# AVR MCU Development Environment Settings Manual

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/avr/

Choose a development tool for your AP01 AVR MCU leaf.

- [Arduino IDE](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/avr/arduino/)
- [PlatformIO IDE](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/avr/platformio/)

Check the model number on your leaf before following a guide. For a different MCU, return to [environment setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/).

# AVR MCU: Arduino IDE Setup

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/avr/arduino/

Set up Arduino IDE for the AP01 AVR MCU leaf and upload a program.

Use Arduino IDE to set up the development environment for the AP01 AVR MCU leaf (ATmega328P, 3.3 V, 8 MHz).

Uploading through AZ01C (USB Type-C) requires a manual reset. See the [AZ01C upload instructions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az01c/#uploading-to-ap01-avr-mcu).

## What to prepare

* Basic Kit
* Data-capable USB cable
* PC (Windows, macOS or Linux)

## Installing Arduino IDE

The Arduino IDE is a development environment for the Arduino, an open source hardware platform for electronics.
The development environment allows you to write programs, write programs to the Arduino board, and display the data coming from the board.
Leafony can be developed with the Arduino IDE.

Let's download the Arduino IDE right away.

1. From the Arduino website, go to `SOFTWARE` and then `DOWNLOADS` to get to the Arduino IDE download page.
2. Download the installer for your OS at the place where it says `Download the Arduino IDE`.
3. Run the downloaded installer and follow the on-screen instructions to install the Arduino IDE.

### Previous IDE releases

Older Arduino IDE installers are available from [Previous IDE Releases](https://www.arduino.cc/en/Main/OldSoftwareReleases#previous).

## Connecting to PC

Connect to your PC with a USB cable.

## Configuration of the microcontroller board

To develop Leafony in the Arduino IDE, let's follow the steps below to configure the IDE.

1. `Arduino AVR Boards` is installed with the IDE. Open `Tools → Board → Boards Manager` to check its version. Use the version selector to install an earlier version.

2. Go to `Tools → Board` and select `Arduino Pro or Pro Mini` and `ATmega328P (3.3V, 8MHz)` for `Processor`.

3. Go to `Tools → Serial Port` and select the serial port that Leafony is connected to. If no port is available, see the [FAQ](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#if-you-cant-find-the-serial-port).

## Checking the operation of the microcontroller board

Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow [Restore the demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#restore-demo).

1. In the Arduino IDE, click on `File → Sketch Examples → 01.Basics → Blink` to open the sample app.
2. The program is written to Leafony by pressing the `write to microcontroller` button.
3. If you can confirm that the LED on the AVR MCU leaf is blinking, you are done.

### Specifying pins for a sketch

The pin should be specified by its name.

[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap01/ap01_pinassign.png)

## Installing Libraries

See [Libraries and board definitions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/) for library sources, the correct ST7032 library for AI04 LCD, and ZIP installation. Add only what your example requires. The initial Blink example needs no additional libraries.

## When in doubt.

If it doesn't work, go to "If it doesn't work..." to find a solution.

:::note[Next]
A number of programs are available in [Sample App](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/).
To make development easier, install the library and get started.
:::

---

# AVR MCU: PlatformIO Setup

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/avr/platformio/

Set up PlatformIO for the AP01 AVR MCU leaf and upload a program.

Use PlatformIO IDE to set up the development environment for the AP01 AVR MCU leaf (ATmega328P, 3.3 V, 8 MHz).

## Introduction

Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is Microsoft's lightweight source-code editor for Windows, macOS, and Linux. PlatformIO IDE is a VS Code extension with fast builds and per-project management of library and board versions.

## What to prepare

- Basic Kit 2
- A Windows, macOS, or Linux computer

## Advance preparation

### Install PlatformIO IDE

1. Install [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/).
2. Open **Extensions**, search for `PlatformIO IDE`, and install the extension published by **PlatformIO**.
3. Wait for setup to finish and restart VS Code if prompted.

PlatformIO Core and the serial monitor are included. A portable Python interpreter is used when available. If prompted to install Python, follow [PlatformIO's instructions](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/faq/install-python.html). Linux also needs `python3-venv`.

Install `Japanese Language Pack for Visual Studio Code` for a Japanese interface or `Teleplot` for plotting only if you need them. See the [official PlatformIO IDE setup guide](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/integration/ide/vscode.html) for details.

## Getting Started

Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow [Restore the demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#restore-demo).

### Create a new project

This Hello World example introduces the PlatformIO IDE workflow.

1. Start VS Code and open **File → New Window**.
2. Select **PlatformIO** in the left sidebar to open **PLATFORMIO QUICK ACCESS**.
3. Select **PIO Home → Open**.
4. Select **New Project** and fill in the Project Wizard, then select **Finish**. The first setup for a board may take several minutes to download its files.
   - Name: `Hello_World_Pjt`
   - Board: `Arduino Pro or Pro Mini ATmega328(3.3v,8Mhz)`
   - Framework: `Arduino`
5. Open `platformio.ini` and check the board and framework settings:

```cpp
[env:pro8MHzatmega328]
platform = atmelavr
board = pro8MHzatmega328
framework = arduino
```

6. The AVR MCU upload workflow detects the serial port automatically, so a COM port number does not need to be specified.
7. Add the serial monitor baud rate to `platformio.ini`:

```cpp
monitor_speed = 115200
```

8. Open `src/main.cpp` and paste the following code. PlatformIO requires `#include <Arduino.h>` at the beginning of an Arduino sketch.

```cpp
#include <Arduino.h>

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(10);
}

void loop(){
  Serial.println("Hello World");
  delay(1000);
}
```

Source code: [Hello_World_Pjt](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/avr/Hello_World_Pjt)

9. Use **Project Environment Switcher** in the bottom PlatformIO toolbar to select the correct active project, then select **Build**.

10. Connect Leafony to the computer as shown in [Connecting to PC](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/avr/arduino/#connecting-to-pc).
11. Select **Upload** to upload the program to the MCU.
12. Press the MCU reset button to run the program.
13. Open **Serial Monitor** and check that `Hello World` appears.

## Install the library

Add only the libraries your example needs to `lib_deps` in the active `[env:...]` section of `platformio.ini`. See [Libraries and board definitions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/) for sources, syntax and existing version specifications. Hello World needs no additional libraries.

## Serial plotter

To plot serial data as in Arduino IDE, use the **Teleplot for VSCode** extension. Download and try the sample below.

1. Download [Teleplot_Example_1](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/avr/Teleplot_Example_1) from GitHub and save it in your project folder.[^1]
2. Run the program.
3. Select **teleplot** at the bottom of the window, choose the COM port, and select **Open** to display the graph.
4. Teleplot plots serial messages in the form `>varName:1234\n`. See the [Teleplot documentation](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=alexnesnes.teleplot) for details.

```cpp
 // Plot a sinus
  Serial.print(">sin:");
  Serial.println(sin(i));

  // Plot a cosinus
  Serial.print(">cos:");
  Serial.println(cos(i));
 ```

## AVR Beginner Examples

Download the sample projects from GitHub, save them in your project folder,[^1] and run them in PlatformIO IDE.

[^1]: The default Windows folder is `C:\Users\<username>\Documents\PlatformIO\Projects`.

| Item | Source code |
| --- | --- |
| [Temperature and humidity sensor](/en/examples/beginner/avr-mcu/basic/temp_humid_sensors/) | [Thermo-Hygrometer_Pjt](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/avr/Thermo-Hygrometer_Pjt) |
| [Illuminance sensor](/en/examples/beginner/avr-mcu/basic/illum_sensor/) | [Illuminance_Meter_Pjt](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/avr/Illuminance_Meter_Pjt) |
| [Accelerometer](/en/examples/beginner/avr-mcu/basic/accelerometer/) | [Accelerometer_Pjt](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/avr/Accelerometer_Pjt) |

## Tips

### MCU and board settings

See [Choose a board definition](/en/environment/libraries/#choose-a-board-definition) for the mapping between AP model numbers and board settings. Follow each MCU's setup page for upload and port configuration.

### Differences from Arduino IDE sketches

1. Add `#include <Arduino.h>` at the beginning of the program. Arduino IDE includes basic type definitions and commonly used headers automatically; PlatformIO requires the explicit include.
2. Define custom functions before they are called, or add a prototype declaration. Arduino IDE prepares declarations automatically, while PlatformIO follows normal C++ rules.

The following example fails to build because the function is defined after its first use:

```cpp
void setup() {
  // put your setup code here, to run once:
  func();

}

void func() {
  ;
}
```

This example builds because the function is defined before its use:

```cpp
void func() {
  ;
}

void setup() {
  // put your setup code here, to run once:
  func();

}
```

This example also builds because it includes a prototype:

```cpp
// Prototypes
void func(void);

void setup() {
  // put your setup code here, to run once:
  func();

}

void func() {
  ;
}
```

### Rename or delete a project folder

**New Project** in the Project Wizard creates a folder under `~/Documents/PlatformIO/Projects` by default. Rename or delete that folder directly in your file manager.

### Change the project folder location

Configure the location from the terminal:

1. Start VS Code and open **File → New Window**.
2. Select **PlatformIO** in the sidebar to open **PLATFORMIO QUICK ACCESS**.
3. Select **PIO Home → Open**.
4. Run `pio settings set projects_dir <absolute-path>` with your desired folder's absolute path.
5. Restart VS Code.

## Reference

- [PlatformIO documentation](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/integration/ide/vscode.html#ide-vscode)

---

Choose a development tool for your AP02 ESP32 MCU leaf.

- [Arduino IDE](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/esp32/arduino/)
- [PlatformIO IDE](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/esp32/platformio/)

# ESP32 MCU: Arduino IDE Setup

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/esp32/arduino/

Set up Arduino IDE for the AP02 ESP32 MCU leaf and upload a program.

Use Arduino IDE to set up the development environment for the AP02 ESP32 MCU leaf (ESP32-WROOM-32).

:::note[Next]
Install the software needed to write a program in Leafony.
:::

## What to prepare

* ESP32 Wi-Fi Kit
* Data-capable USB cable
* PC (Windows, macOS or Linux)

## Installing Arduino IDE

1. Open the [Arduino website](https://www.arduino.cc/) and go to **SOFTWARE**.
2. Download the installer for your operating system.
3. Run the installer and follow its instructions.

### Previous IDE releases

Older versions are available from [Previous IDE Releases](https://www.arduino.cc/en/Main/OldSoftwareReleases#previous).

:::note[Next]
Let's write a program in Leafony and make it work!
:::

## Connecting to PC

Connect to your PC with a USB cable.

## Configuration of the microcontroller board

Follow [Espressif’s official installation guide](https://docs.espressif.com/projects/arduino-esp32/en/latest/installing.html) for the package distribution URL. If an example specifies a core version, use that version.

To use the ESP32 MCU leaf with the Arduino IDE, you need to install Arduino core for the ESP32.

1. Open the `File → Preferences` in the Arduino IDE and enter the following URL in the `Additional Board Manager URL:` field.

　　`https://espressif.github.io/arduino-esp32/package_esp32_index.json`

2. Select `Tools -> Board -> Board Manager`, search for `esp32 by Espressif Systems` and press the Install button. Use the version selector if you need to select a specific version.

3. Choose `Tools → Board → ESP32 Dev Module`.
4. Choose the connected serial port from `Tools → Serial Port`. If it is not listed, see [Serial port not found](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#if-you-cant-find-the-serial-port).

## Checking the operation of the microcontroller board

Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow [Restore the demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#restore-demo).

Let's write a Sample App and get the ESP32 Wi-Fi Kit running.

1. Launch the Arduino.
2. Paste the following sample code into your code editor.

```c++
//*****************************
// ボタン入力の状態をシリアルモニタに表示するサンプル
//*****************************
int pushButton = 0;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  pinMode(pushButton, INPUT);
}

void loop() {
  int buttonState = digitalRead(pushButton);
  Serial.println(buttonState);
  delay(1);
}
```

3. Select the COM port to which the ESP32 leaf is connected.
4. Push the `write to microcomputer board` button to write a sketch.
5. Press and hold the `Boot mode switch` on the ESP32 leaf when the following message appears during the writing process.

6. Open the serial monitor and set the communication speed to `115200bps`.
7. Press the `Boot mode switch (IO0)` and see if the input state of the switch changes.

[](https://docs.leafony.com/environment/esp32/arduino/ap02_tips.png)

### Specifying pins for a sketch
**Pin should be specified by Port, not Name.**
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap02/ap02_pinassign_v1.png)

#### Restrictions
※1：Output cannot be set
※2：①For UART1, the pin number is set to RX=26 and TX=25. For UART0 and UART2, the pin number is not specified.

```c++
HardwareSerial Serial1(1); // UART1 (RX=9, TX=10)

void setup() {
  Serial1.begin(9600, SERIAL_8N1, 26, 25); // ピンを変更 (RX=26, TX=25)
}
```
　　②Cannot be used as analog input if WiFi.h is included

※3: Pull-up prohibited because it is used for bootstrapping

## Installing Libraries

Install only the libraries required by your example. See [Libraries and board definitions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/) for sources and installation steps. The button-input example above needs no additional libraries.

## When in doubt.

If it doesn't work, go to "If it doesn't work..." to find a solution.

:::note[Next]
A number of programs are available in [Sample App](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples).
To make development easier, install the library and get started.
:::

---

# ESP32 MCU: PlatformIO Setup

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/esp32/platformio/

Set up PlatformIO for the AP02 ESP32 MCU leaf and upload a program.

Use PlatformIO IDE to set up the development environment for the AP02 ESP32 MCU leaf (ESP32-WROOM-32).

## Introduction

Visual Studio Code (VS Code) is Microsoft's lightweight source-code editor for Windows, macOS, and Linux. PlatformIO IDE is a VS Code extension with fast builds and per-project management of library and board versions.

## What to prepare

- ESP32 Wi-Fi Kit 2
- A Windows, macOS, or Linux computer

## Advance preparation

### Install PlatformIO IDE

1. Install [VS Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/).
2. Open **Extensions**, search for `PlatformIO IDE`, and install the extension published by **PlatformIO**.
3. Wait for setup to finish and restart VS Code if prompted.

PlatformIO Core and the serial monitor are included. A portable Python interpreter is used when available. If prompted to install Python, follow [PlatformIO's instructions](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/faq/install-python.html). Linux also needs `python3-venv`.

Install `Japanese Language Pack for Visual Studio Code` for a Japanese interface or `Teleplot` for plotting only if you need them. See the [official PlatformIO IDE setup guide](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/integration/ide/vscode.html) for details.

## Getting Started

Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow [Restore the demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#restore-demo).

### Create a new project

This Hello World example introduces the PlatformIO IDE workflow.

1. Start VS Code and open **File → New Window**.
2. Select **PlatformIO** in the left sidebar to open **PLATFORMIO QUICK ACCESS**.
3. Select **PIO Home → Open**.
4. Select **New Project** and fill in the Project Wizard, then select **Finish**. The first setup for a board may take several minutes to download its files.
   - Name: `ESP32_Hello_World_Pjt`
   - Board: `Espressif ESP32 Dev Module`
   - Framework: `Arduino`
5. Open `platformio.ini` and check the board and framework settings:

```cpp
[env:esp32dev]
platform = espressif32
board = esp32dev
framework = arduino
```

6. The ESP32 MCU upload workflow detects the serial port automatically, so a COM port number does not need to be specified.
7. Add the serial monitor baud rate to `platformio.ini`:

```cpp
monitor_speed = 115200
```

8. Open `src/main.cpp` and paste the following code. PlatformIO requires `#include <Arduino.h>` at the beginning of an Arduino sketch.

```cpp
#include <Arduino.h>

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  delay(10);
}

void loop(){
  Serial.println("Hello World");
  delay(1000);
}
```

Source code: [ESP32_Hello_World_Pjt](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/esp32/ESP32_Hello_World_Pjt)

9. Use **Project Environment Switcher** in the bottom PlatformIO toolbar to select the correct active project, then select **Build**.

10. Connect Leafony to the computer as shown in [Connecting to PC](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/esp32/arduino/#connecting-to-pc).
11. Select **Upload** to upload the program to the MCU.
12. Press the MCU reset button to run the program.
13. Open **Serial Monitor** and check that `Hello World` appears.

## Install the library

Add only the libraries your example needs to `lib_deps` in the active `[env:...]` section of `platformio.ini`. See [Libraries and board definitions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/) for sources, syntax and existing version specifications. Hello World needs no additional libraries.

## Serial plotter

To plot serial data as in Arduino IDE, use the **Teleplot for VSCode** extension. Download and try the sample below.

1. Download [ESP32_Teleplot_Example_1](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/esp32/ESP32_Teleplot_Example_1) from GitHub and save it in your project folder.[^1]
2. Run the program.
3. Select **teleplot** at the bottom of the window, choose the COM port, and select **Open** to display the graph.
4. Teleplot plots serial messages in the form `>varName:1234\n`. See the [Teleplot documentation](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=alexnesnes.teleplot) for details.

```cpp
 // Plot a sinus
  Serial.print(">sin:");
  Serial.println(sin(i));

  // Plot a cosinus
  Serial.print(">cos:");
  Serial.println(cos(i));
 ```

The following example fails to build because the function is defined after its first use:

```cpp

  func();

}

  ;
}
```

This example builds because the function is defined before its use:

```cpp
void func() {
  ;
}

void setup() {
  // put your setup code here, to run once:
  func();

}
```

This example also builds because it includes a prototype:

```cpp
// Prototypes
```

# Libraries and board definitions

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/

Choose board definitions for your Leafony MCU and find the libraries and installation methods used by the examples.

To upload a program, select the **board definition for your MCU** and the **libraries needed by your leaves and example**. First run the initial program in [development environment setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/), then add the libraries you need.

## Choose a board definition

| Leaf | Arduino IDE | PlatformIO |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AP01 AVR MCU | `Arduino AVR Boards` → `Arduino Pro or Pro Mini` → `ATmega328P (3.3V,8MHz)`. [Setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/avr/arduino/) | `platform = atmelavr`, `board = pro8MHzatmega328`. [Setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/avr/platformio/) |
| AP02 ESP32 MCU | `esp32 by Espressif Systems` → `ESP32 Dev Module`. [Setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/esp32/arduino/) | `platform = espressif32`, `board = esp32dev`. [Setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/esp32/platformio/) |
| AP03 STM32 MCU | Use Leafony's board package. [URL and setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/arduino_ide/) | Use the latest stable version of `ststm32` with `platform = ststm32` and `board = leafony_ap03`. [Installation and upload settings](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/platformio/) |

For AP03 in PlatformIO, also follow the linked instructions to set the upload tool and port. For AP01, the reset procedure depends on the USB leaf model; also check the [AZ01C instructions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az01c/#uploading-to-ap01-avr-mcu) if you use it.

[AP03B](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03b/) and [AP05](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap05/) are different models. Before reusing the settings above, check each model's documentation for available software and connection requirements.

## Choose the libraries you need

These are the main sources referenced by the published examples. **You do not need to install them all.** Follow the example's leaf and library requirements and the distributed project's `platformio.ini`. A row does not mean that every library in it works with every MCU or leaf.

| Leaf or function | Source / header | What to check |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shared 4-Sensors functions | [Adafruit Unified Sensor](https://github.com/adafruit/Adafruit_Sensor) / `Adafruit_Sensor.h`, [Adafruit BusIO](https://github.com/adafruit/Adafruit_BusIO) / `Adafruit_BusIO_Register.h` | Also check dependencies required by the sensor library |
| HTS221 temperature and humidity | [SmartEverything HTS221](https://github.com/ameltech/sme-hts221-library) / `HTS221.h` | Use the implementation specified by the example |
| OPT3001 illuminance | [ClosedCube OPT3001](https://registry.platformio.org/libraries/closedcube/ClosedCube%20OPT3001) / `ClosedCube_OPT3001.h` | Search Arduino Library Manager for `ClosedCube OPT3001` |
| AI01 acceleration (LIS2DHTR) | [Adafruit LIS3DH](https://github.com/adafruit/Adafruit_LIS3DH) / `Adafruit_LIS3DH.h` | The published examples use Adafruit LIS3DH. This is not for AI05's LIS2DW12 |
| BLE leaf | [TBGLib](https://github.com/Leafony/TBGLib) / `TBGLib.h` | Separate from libraries for ESP32's built-in BLE |
| AI04 LCD | [tomozh/arduino_ST7032](https://github.com/tomozh/arduino_ST7032) / `ST7032.h` | See the [AI04 notes](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/#st7032-library-for-ai04-lcd) below |
| RTC on RTC & microSD | [RTClib](https://github.com/adafruit/RTClib) / `RTClib.h` | Separate from the STM32 internal RTC library |
| AVR timer interrupts | [MsTimer2](https://github.com/PaulStoffregen/MsTimer2) / `MsTimer2.h` | For STM32, see [HardwareTimer](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/arduino_ide/#hardwaretimer) |
| STM32 internal RTC and low power | [STM32RTC](https://github.com/stm32duino/STM32RTC) / `STM32RTC.h`, [STM32LowPower](https://github.com/stm32duino/STM32LowPower) / `STM32LowPower.h` | Check [Arduino Core compatibility](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/platformio/#library-versions-in-older-samples) |
| Existing cellular communication (Cat-M1) examples | [LteLeafV4](https://github.com/Leafony/LteLeafV4) / `LteLeafV4.h` | Match the communication leaf model to the example |
| Wi-Fi Mary | [WiFi101Leafony](https://github.com/Leafony/WiFi101Leafony) / `WiFi101Leafony.h` | Separate from settings for AP02's built-in Wi-Fi |
| LoRa and signed communication | [arduino-LoRa](https://github.com/Leafony/arduino-LoRa) / `LoRa.h`, [arduino-tca9536](https://github.com/Leafony/arduino-tca9536) / `TCA9536.h`, [SparkFun ATECCX08a](https://github.com/sparkfun/SparkFun_ATECCX08a_Arduino_Library) / `SparkFun_ATECCX08a_Arduino_Library.h` | Follow the example for the communication leaf and function you use |

The cellular examples in the table use Cat-M1, an IoT communication technology that runs on mobile operators' LTE networks.

### ST7032 library for AI04 LCD

The published AI04 examples use **`arduino_ST7032` by tomozh**. `LCD_ST7032` and `ST7032_asukiaaa` are different implementations. For Arduino IDE, download the ZIP from the source and install it as described below.

If you see `ST7032.h: No such file or directory`, check the installation. Installing the library does not enable LCD power. See [AI04 power and initialization](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai04/#powering-and-initializing-the-lcd) and the [LCD example for your MCU](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/).

## Install in Arduino IDE

1. Check the library name, author and version specified by the example.
2. If available in Library Manager, open **Tools → Manage Libraries**, search by name, check the author and version, and install it.
3. For ZIP distributions, download the file using **Code → Download ZIP** or the source's download link, then import it with **Sketch → Include Library → Add .ZIP Library**.
4. Compile the example. If a header is missing, compare the filename in the error with the library you installed.

See [Arduino's library installation instructions](https://support.arduino.cc/hc/en-us/articles/5145457742236-Install-libraries-in-the-Arduino-IDE) for details.

## Install in PlatformIO

Add `lib_deps` **inside the `[env:...]` section you use** in `platformio.ini`. If it already exists, add entries to the same list. Dependencies are downloaded during the build. If the example includes a complete configuration file, use its settings.

```ini
; Syntax example. Hello World does not need additional libraries.
lib_deps =
    adafruit/Adafruit Unified Sensor
    adafruit/Adafruit BusIO
```

Installing from a GitHub URL also requires [Git](https://git-scm.com/downloads). Restart VS Code after installing it and check that `git --version` works in a terminal. See [PlatformIO's `lib_deps` reference](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/projectconf/sections/env/options/library/lib_deps.html) for syntax.

### Versions in existing examples

Earlier lists included the following dependencies. They help you interpret existing projects. Before copying them into a new project, check the example and Arduino Core compatibility.

| Library | Existing PlatformIO dependency example |
| --- | --- |
| Adafruit Unified Sensor | `adafruit/Adafruit Unified Sensor@^1.1.6` |
| Adafruit BusIO | `adafruit/Adafruit BusIO@^1.14.1` |
| ClosedCube OPT3001 | `closedcube/ClosedCube OPT3001@^1.1.2` |
| Adafruit LIS3DH | `adafruit/Adafruit LIS3DH@1.1.2` |
| AI04 LCD | `tomozh/ST7032@0.0.0-alpha+sha.501bf64fe6` |
| MsTimer2 | `paulstoffregen/MsTimer2@^1.1` |
| RTClib | `adafruit/RTClib@^2.1.1` |
| STM32RTC (Core 2.x) | `stm32duino/STM32duino RTC@1.2.0` |
| STM32LowPower (Core 2.x) | `stm32duino/STM32duino Low Power@^1.2.2` |

The STM32RTC and STM32LowPower entries above are for STM32 Arduino Core 2.x. The latest stable `ststm32` uses Core 3.x, so new projects specify 2.x of both libraries.

```ini
; For STM32 Arduino Core 3.x
lib_deps =
    stm32duino/STM32duino RTC@^2.0.0
    stm32duino/STM32duino Low Power@^2.0.0
```

To find your Core version, see [matching the STM32 Arduino Core version](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/platformio/#library-versions-in-older-samples). If a build changes after a library update, check the full error, board package and library versions, and include them in the [question template](https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/ask/#question-template).

# STM32 MCU: Arduino IDE Setup

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/arduino_ide/

Set up Arduino IDE for the AP03 STM32 MCU leaf and upload a program.

## What to prepare

- STM32 MCU leaf (AP03 / STM32L452REI6)
- Basic Kit
- A Windows, macOS, or Linux computer

## Installing STM32CubeProg

Install [STM32CubeProg](https://www.stmcu.jp/design/sw_dev/pc_soft/58442/) to upload programs to the MCU.[^1] The linked download information is in Japanese.

## Installing the Arduino IDE

1. Open the [Arduino software download page](https://www.arduino.cc/en/software/).
2. Under **Downloads**, select the installer for your operating system.
3. Follow the installer instructions. See the [installation walkthrough (Japanese)](https://www.indoorcorgielec.com/resources/arduinoide%E8%A8%AD%E5%AE%9A/arduino-ide%E3%81%AE%E3%82%A4%E3%83%B3%E3%82%B9%E3%83%88%E3%83%BC%E3%83%AB%E3%81%A8%E8%A8%AD%E5%AE%9A/) for more detail.

### Previous IDE releases

Older versions are available from [Previous IDE Releases](https://www.arduino.cc/en/Main/OldSoftwareReleases#previous).

## Connect to PC

Connect Leafony to your computer using a USB cable.

## Configuration of the microcontroller board

1. Install the board package distributed by [Leafony STM32](https://github.com/Leafony/BoardManagerFiles). Open **File → Preferences** and add the following to **Additional Boards Manager URLs**.[^2]

`https://github.com/Leafony/BoardManagerFiles/raw/master/Leafony_STM32_v3/package_leafony_stm_index.json`

2. Open **Tools → Board → Boards Manager**.
3. Search for `Leafony` and install it. Installation may take several minutes. The `Leafony_STM32_v3` package distributes version `1.9.2-R00` (checked September 15, 2026).

4. Select **Tools → Board → Leafony STM32**.

5. Select **Tools → Board part number → Leafony STM32 MCU**. The default clock is 80 MHz; a 16 MHz board option is also provided for lower-power operation.

6. Select the connected port under **Tools → Serial Port**. If no port is available, see [Serial port not found](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#if-you-cant-find-the-serial-port).

## Checking the operation of the microcontroller board

Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow [Restore the demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#restore-demo).

1. Set the STM32 MCU **program switch** to **Program**, then press the **reset switch**.

[See the AP03 Program / Run and Reset illustrated guide](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03/#program-run)

2. Follow the [temperature and humidity sensor example](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/beginner/stm32-mcu/basic/temp_humid_sensors/) to upload the program. Uploading may take some time. A successful upload displays `Start operation achieved successfully`. If that message is absent, the program will not run correctly.[^3]

3. When uploading finishes, return the **program switch** to **Run**. The LED turns off.
4. Press the **reset switch** to start the program. Check that temperature and humidity values appear.

### Specifying pins for a sketch

With this Leafony board definition, specify pins by Name or Port.

[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap03/ap03_pinassign.png)

## Installing libraries

Install the libraries required by your example from [Libraries and board definitions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/). Check the board package and Arduino Core version before selecting STM32RTC and STM32LowPower versions.

The timer-interrupt library `MsTimer2.h` is for AVR MCU and cannot be used with STM32 MCU. Use HardwareTimer as described below.

### HardwareTimer

See the [HardwareTimer documentation](https://github.com/stm32duino/wiki/wiki/HardwareTimer-library) for details. This is an example of initialization:

```c++
HardwareTimer *timer2 = new HardwareTimer (TIM2);

  timer2->setOverflow(LOOP_INTERVAL, MICROSEC_FORMAT);       // 125ms
  timer2->attachInterrupt(intTimer);
  timer2->resume();
```

Interrupt routine:

```c++
void intTimer(void){
  bInterval = true;
　：
　：
}
```

## When in doubt

See the [FAQ](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/) for troubleshooting.

[^1]: Historical testing recorded Windows 64-bit with versions 2.12.0, 2.6.0, and 2.4.0. Version 2.5.0 did not work in that testing.
[^2]: The Boards Manager URL changed when the package was updated from `Leafony_STM32` to `Leafony_STM32_v3`. See the [Leafony board package README](https://github.com/Leafony/BoardManagerFiles/blob/master/README.md).
[^3]: If uploading is attempted without setting the switch to Program, the IDE may still display `Writing to the board is complete`, while the output below contains `Timeout error occured while waiting for acknowledgement`. The program will not run correctly.

---

# STM32 MCU: PlatformIO Setup

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/platformio/

Set up PlatformIO for the AP03 STM32 MCU leaf and upload a program.

## Introduction

This guide follows the [Japanese STM32 PlatformIO guide](https://docs.leafony.com/environment/stm32/platformio/) and uses VS Code with PlatformIO to build a program that prints `Hello World` once per second. STM32CubeProgrammer uploads it through a USB leaf. You do not need Arduino IDE or its board package for this workflow.

Install the latest stable software from the official distribution sites. The STM32CubeProgrammer version pins in older instructions are no longer required for this workflow.

## Required items

- STM32 MCU leaf (AP03 / STM32L452REI6) and a USB leaf
- A data-capable USB cable
- A Windows, macOS or Linux computer with an internet connection

For Basic Kit 2, replace the assembled AVR MCU with the STM32 MCU leaf before programming.

## Install the tools

1. Install [Visual Studio Code](https://code.visualstudio.com/download) for your OS and CPU.
2. Open Extensions in VS Code, find **PlatformIO IDE** published by **PlatformIO**, and install it. Wait for its initial setup to finish and restart VS Code if requested.
3. Install [STM32CubeProgrammer from ST](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeprog.html). Locate its command-line executable; you will use its actual path in `upload_command`.

PlatformIO Core and its serial monitor are included in the IDE extension. If prompted for Python, follow [PlatformIO's Python installation instructions](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/faq/install-python.html); Linux also requires `python3-venv`. See the [PlatformIO IDE documentation](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/integration/ide/vscode.html) for setup details.

Python is prepared automatically on supported operating systems. Add `Japanese Language Pack for Visual Studio Code` if you want a Japanese interface, or [Teleplot](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/platformio/#serial-plotter) for graphs.

| OS | STM32CubeProgrammer command-line tool |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | `bin/STM32_Programmer_CLI.exe` under the installation folder |
| macOS | `Contents/Resources/bin/STM32_Programmer_CLI` inside `STM32CubeProgrammer.app` |
| Linux | `bin/STM32_Programmer.sh` under the installation folder |

Use a local project path with simple ASCII characters, such as `C:/PlatformIO/Projects` on Windows. Open the command terminal through **PlatformIO → Quick Access → Miscellaneous → PlatformIO Core CLI**. To change the default folder for new projects, run the following with your actual path and restart VS Code:

```sh
pio settings set projects_dir "C:/PlatformIO/Projects"
```

This does not move existing projects. See the [`projects_dir` documentation](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/core/userguide/cmd_settings.html#projects-dir).

Simple paths help avoid path-handling problems. User folders and OneDrive locations differ between computers, so check the actual destination before copying an example. On macOS and Linux, replace the quoted path with the absolute path to your chosen folder.

### Install the latest ST STM32 platform

Install PlatformIO's **ST STM32 (`ststm32`)** development platform. For AP03, use its built-in [Leafony Systems AP03](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/boards/ststm32/leafony_ap03.html) board definition.

Run this command in PlatformIO Core CLI. Omitting the version installs the latest stable release from PlatformIO Registry.

```sh
pio pkg install --global --platform "platformio/ststm32"
```

If ST STM32 is already installed, update it to the latest release with:

```sh
pio pkg update --global --platform "platformio/ststm32"
```

Packages required by the project, including the Arduino framework, are installed automatically during the first build. See [`pio pkg install`](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/core/userguide/pkg/cmd_install.html), [`pio pkg update`](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/core/userguide/pkg/cmd_update.html), and the [ST STM32 releases](https://github.com/platformio/platform-ststm32/releases) for details.

## Quick start

Uploading replaces the program currently on the MCU. To run the kit demo again later, follow [Restore the demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#restore-demo).

### 1. Create the project

1. Create an empty folder named `STM32_Hello_World_Pjt` and open it with **File → Open Folder** in VS Code.
2. Create `platformio.ini` and a `src` folder in the project root, then create `main.cpp` inside `src`. Their contents are provided in the steps below.

```text
STM32_Hello_World_Pjt/
├── platformio.ini
└── src/
    └── main.cpp
```

### 2. Identify the serial port

With USB disconnected, assemble the STM32 MCU and USB leaves as shown in the [connection example](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/arduino_ide/#connect-to-pc). Connect the USB leaf to your computer, then run:

```sh
pio device list
```

The connected port disappears and reappears when you unplug and reconnect the cable.

| OS | Example port |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | `COM3` |
| macOS | `/dev/cu.usbserial-XXXXXXXX` |
| Linux | `/dev/ttyUSB0` |

If no port appears, check the cable, leaf connections and USB driver. Refer to the [FAQ](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/). On Linux, also follow [PlatformIO's serial port permissions instructions](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/core/installation/udev-rules.html).

### 3. Configure platformio.ini

The following example is for Windows on `COM3`. Replace the port and executable path with those on your computer.

```ini
[env:leafony_ap03]
platform = ststm32
board = leafony_ap03
framework = arduino

upload_protocol = custom
upload_port = COM3
upload_command = "C:/Program Files/STMicroelectronics/STM32Cube/STM32CubeProgrammer/bin/STM32_Programmer_CLI.exe" -c port=$UPLOAD_PORT br=115200 -w "$SOURCE" 0x08000000 -v

monitor_port = ${this.upload_port}
monitor_speed = 115200
```

On macOS, replace `upload_port` and `upload_command` with the following, using the actual port name:

```ini
upload_port = /dev/cu.usbserial-XXXXXXXX
upload_command = "/Applications/STMicroelectronics/STM32Cube/STM32CubeProgrammer/STM32CubeProgrammer.app/Contents/Resources/bin/STM32_Programmer_CLI" -c port=$UPLOAD_PORT br=115200 -w "$SOURCE" 0x08000000 -v
```

On Linux, use the absolute installation path and actual serial port. This example uses the account name `user`:

```ini
upload_port = /dev/ttyUSB0
upload_command = "/home/user/STMicroelectronics/STM32Cube/STM32CubeProgrammer/bin/STM32_Programmer.sh" -c port=$UPLOAD_PORT br=115200 -w "$SOURCE" 0x08000000 -v
```

| Setting | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `[env:leafony_ap03]` | Names the build environment and output folder |
| `platform = ststm32` | Uses ST STM32 without a version pin |
| `board = leafony_ap03` | Selects the built-in Leafony Systems AP03 board definition; use lowercase |
| `framework = arduino` | Uses the Arduino framework supported by ST STM32 |
| `upload_protocol = custom` | Runs `upload_command` for uploads |
| `$UPLOAD_PORT`, `$SOURCE` | Substituted by PlatformIO with the port and firmware path |
| `0x08000000` | Flash start address |
| `-v` | Verifies the uploaded data |
| `monitor_port` | Serial monitor port; the upload port in this example |
| `monitor_speed` | Serial baud rate; must match `Serial.begin()` |

Leave `$UPLOAD_PORT` and `$SOURCE` unchanged. See the [PlatformIO upload command reference](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/projectconf/sections/env/options/upload/upload_command.html) and [STM32CubeProgrammer CLI manual](https://dev.st.com/stm32cube-docs/prog/2.23.0/en/docs/markup/CubeProg_Command_Lines.html).

### 4. Write the program

Save the following as `src/main.cpp`:

```cpp
#include <Arduino.h>

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
}

void loop() {
  Serial.println("Hello World");
  delay(1000);
}
```

### 5. Build

Run **PlatformIO → PROJECT TASKS → leafony_ap03 → General → Build**, or run this command in the project folder:

```sh
pio run -e leafony_ap03
```

The first build downloads the compiler and framework and can take several minutes. Check for `SUCCESS` at the end of the log and the generated file `.pio/build/leafony_ap03/firmware.bin`. If the project is not recognized, reopen the folder containing `platformio.ini`.

If several projects or build environments are open, check that the selected target is `leafony_ap03` in `STM32_Hello_World_Pjt`.

### 6. Upload to the STM32 MCU

1. Close any application using the serial port, including the serial monitor and Teleplot. Press `Ctrl+C` in PlatformIO's monitor terminal to stop it.
2. Set the STM32 MCU switch to **Program** and check that its LED is on.
3. **Press Reset** to enter programming mode.
4. Run **PROJECT TASKS → leafony_ap03 → General → Upload**, or:

```sh
pio run -e leafony_ap03 -t upload
```

[See the AP03 Program / Run and Reset illustrated guide](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03/#program-run)

Check the STM32CubeProgrammer log for successful connection, programming and verification. A verification success message may read `Download verified successfully`; wording depends on the tool version. If there is a timeout or verification error, close other port users, reset in Program mode and upload again, even if the overall log says `SUCCESS`.

### 7. Check Hello World

1. Set the switch back to **Run** and check that the LED turns off.
2. **Press Reset** to start the program.
3. Run **PROJECT TASKS → leafony_ap03 → General → Monitor**, or:

```sh
pio device monitor -e leafony_ap03
```

The following output should appear once per second:

```text
Hello World
Hello World
Hello World
```

## Use an existing sample

Download a project from the [Leafony STM32 PlatformIO samples](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/stm32). Open the individual folder containing its `platformio.ini`, rather than the entire repository.

Use the same platform, board and upload settings as in the quick start. For example, when using [STM32_Hello_World_Pjt](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/stm32/STM32_Hello_World_Pjt), set `platform = ststm32`, `board = leafony_ap03` and `framework = arduino` in `platformio.ini`, then configure the upload tool and port as described above. Review and preserve sample-specific `lib_deps` and `build_flags`.

Replace old upload commands referencing `Arduino15/.../STM32Tools/1.4.0/...` with the path to your installed STM32CubeProgrammer.

To update an existing project's ST STM32 platform to the latest release, replace a version constraint such as `platform = ststm32@...` with `platform = ststm32`. Review [library compatibility](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/platformio/#library-versions-in-older-samples) and adjust library version constraints as needed, then run the following in the project folder:

```sh
pio pkg update
```

Dependencies are updated within the version constraints in `platformio.ini`; see the [`pio pkg update` reference](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/core/userguide/pkg/cmd_update.html).

## Libraries

Add libraries to [`lib_deps`](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/projectconf/sections/env/options/library/lib_deps.html) inside the `[env:...]` section you use. The Hello World example needs no additional libraries.

If `lib_deps` already exists, append to its list. Add only the libraries needed for the leaves and functions you use.

```ini
lib_deps =
    adafruit/Adafruit Unified Sensor
    adafruit/Adafruit BusIO
    https://github.com/Leafony/TBGLib
```

Git URLs require [Git](https://git-scm.com/downloads). Restart VS Code after installing it and check that `git --version` works in the terminal.

See [Libraries and board definitions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/) for the source catalog. Check STM32 Core and library compatibility below.

### Library versions in older samples

[ST STM32 20.0.0](https://github.com/platformio/platform-ststm32/releases/tag/v20.0.0) moved to STM32 Arduino Core 3.0.0. Follow the [STM32RTC requirements](https://github.com/stm32duino/STM32RTC#requirement) and [STM32LowPower requirements](https://github.com/stm32duino/STM32LowPower#requirement): use the 2.x library lines with Core 3.x, and 1.x with Core 2.x.

```ini
; For STM32 Arduino Core 3.x
lib_deps =
    stm32duino/STM32duino RTC@^2.0.0
    stm32duino/STM32duino Low Power@^2.0.0
```

Check the `framework-arduinoststm32` entry under `PACKAGES` in the build log to identify your Core. Do not use the AVR `MsTimer2` library on STM32; use [HardwareTimer](https://github.com/stm32duino/Arduino_Core_STM32/wiki/HardwareTimer-library) instead.

Even if an older sample specifies a version such as `@1.2.0`, check each library's README against the Arduino Core used by your project.

## Serial plotter

Install [Teleplot for VSCode](https://marketplace.visualstudio.com/items?itemName=alexnesnes.teleplot). Upload this example, return the switch to Run and reset:

```cpp
#include <Arduino.h>

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
}

void loop() {
  Serial.print(">seconds:");
  Serial.println(millis() / 1000.0f);
  delay(100);
}
```

Close PlatformIO's serial monitor. From the VS Code command palette run **teleplot: Start teleplot session**, choose the serial port and baud rate `115200`, then click **Open**. Check that `seconds` appears in the graph.

Teleplot uses newline-terminated `>name:value` messages. `Serial.println()` supplies the newline. Close Teleplot's port before uploading another program. See also the [STM32 Teleplot example](https://github.com/Leafony/platformio-sample-projects/tree/main/stm32/STM32_Teleplot_Example_1).

## Port an Arduino IDE sketch

`src/main.cpp` follows normal C++ rules. Add `#include <Arduino.h>`, declare functions before use, and add required libraries to `lib_deps`.

```cpp
#include <Arduino.h>

void printMessage();

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  printMessage();
}

void loop() {
}

void printMessage() {
  Serial.println("Hello World");
}
```

## Upload with the STM32CubeProgrammer GUI

1. Build and locate `.pio/build/leafony_ap03/firmware.bin`. If you renamed the environment, use its folder name instead.
2. Close other serial port users, switch to Program and press Reset.
3. Open STM32CubeProgrammer and connect using the following settings.

| Setting | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Connection | UART |
| Port | The STM32 MCU serial port |
| Baud rate | 115200 |
| Parity | Even |
| Data bits | 8 |
| Stop bits | 1 |
| Flow control | OFF |

4. Open **Erasing & Programming**. Select `firmware.bin` and start address `0x08000000`.
5. Enable **Verify programming**, click **Start Programming**, and check that verification succeeds.
6. Click **Disconnect**, return the switch to Run, press Reset, and check output in PlatformIO's serial monitor.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | Check |
| --- | --- |
| `UnknownBoard` or missing variant files | Use lowercase `board = leafony_ap03` and update ST STM32 to the latest release |
| `pio` command not found | Reopen the PlatformIO Core CLI terminal |
| Upload tool not found | Actual installation path and quotes around paths containing spaces |
| Cannot open the port | Port name, other applications holding the port, and Linux permissions |
| Connection times out | Program switch, Reset before upload, USB cable and port name |
| No output after upload | Switch back to Run, Reset, and `monitor_port` |
| Garbled serial output | Match `monitor_speed` to `Serial.begin()`; this example uses 115200 |

---

# STM32 MCU: STM32CubeIDE Setup

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/stm32cube_ide/

Build an AP03 STM32 Hello World project, upload it over UART and check serial output.

## Introduction

Use the Eclipse-based STM32CubeIDE to build a program for **AP03 / STM32L452REI6**, upload it using STM32CubeProgrammer, and display `Hello World` every second over a serial connection. For a first Arduino sketch, use the [Arduino IDE](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/arduino_ide/) or [PlatformIO](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/platformio/) guide instead.

The original screenshots and workspace names use STM32CubeIDE 1.11.2. From version 2.0.0, **STM32CubeMX is a separate tool**: configure peripherals and generate the project there, then open it in STM32CubeIDE. See [ST's release announcement](https://community.st.com/stm32cubeide-mcus-28/stm32cubeide-2-0-0-released-159542). Use the branch below that matches your tools.

## What to prepare

- AP03 STM32 MCU, a USB leaf, and a data-capable USB cable (swap the AVR MCU if using Basic Kit 2)
- A computer supported by the tools below
- STM32CubeIDE, STM32CubeMX for project generation, and STM32CubeProgrammer
- A serial terminal such as Tera Term on Windows

## Preparation

### Install the STM32CubeIDE

Download the Eclipse-based edition from the [ST product page](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeide.html) and follow the installer for your OS. Install [STM32CubeMX](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubemx.html) separately for the 2.x workflow. Use the installation requirements for the version you selected.

### Install STM32CubeProgrammer

Install [STM32CubeProgrammer](https://www.st.com/en/development-tools/stm32cubeprog.html) for UART uploads through the USB leaf.

### Install a serial terminal

For Windows, obtain Tera Term from the [official project](https://github.com/TeraTermProject/teraterm). On macOS or Linux, use a serial terminal that can select the connected port and a baud rate of 115200.

## Quick start

You can start from the [existing Hello_World project](https://github.com/Leafony/STM32CubeIDE-Sample-Software/tree/main/Hello_World) using [Import a project](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/stm32cube_ide/#import-a-project), or generate your own project as follows.

### Create a project

1. **For CubeIDE 2.x:** open STM32CubeMX and create a project for MCU `STM32L452REI6`. **For the original 1.x integrated UI:** choose **File → New → STM32 Project**, use **MCU/MPU Selector**, enter `STM32L452REI6` in **Commercial Part Number**, then select the device.
2. Name the project `Hello_World` and choose a local folder. With separate CubeMX, select `STM32CubeIDE` as the toolchain. With the original integrated wizard, the example used C++, Executable and STM32Cube.
3. Continue with peripheral settings below. Generate the project from CubeMX or the integrated UI, then open it in STM32CubeIDE.

### Configure the device and generate initialization code

1. In **Pinout & Configuration**, assign `PA2` to `USART2_TX` and `PA3` to `USART2_RX`.
2. Open **Connectivity → USART2**, choose **Asynchronous**, disable hardware flow control, and set the baud rate to `115200`.

3. Generate code and open the generated `main.c`. Locate it in the project tree; source and build-output folders serve different purposes.

### Add the code

Add code in the matching `USER CODE` blocks so you can identify it when regenerating code. Line numbers depend on the tool version and generated configuration.

Include the standard I/O header:

```c
/* USER CODE BEGIN Includes */
#include <stdio.h>
/* USER CODE END Includes */
```

Before calling `printf`, disable output buffering:

```c
/* USER CODE BEGIN 1 */
setbuf(stdout, NULL);
/* USER CODE END 1 */
```

Inside the generated main loop, print once per second:

```c
/* USER CODE BEGIN 3 */
printf("Hello World\r\n");
HAL_Delay(1000);
```

Add `_write` to send `printf` output through USART2:

```c
/* USER CODE BEGIN 4 */
int _write(int file, char *ptr, int len)
{
  HAL_UART_Transmit(&huart2, (uint8_t *)ptr, len, 10);
  return len;
}
/* USER CODE END 4 */
```

Choose **Project → Build All**. Fix any build errors and locate the generated `Hello_World.elf` in the active build output folder, commonly `Debug`. Use the actual filename and path from your project.

### Upload with STM32CubeProgrammer

Uploading replaces the program on the MCU. See [Restore the demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/#restore-demo) if you want to run the kit demo again later.

1. Connect the USB leaf as shown in [Connect to PC](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/arduino_ide/#connect-to-pc). Set AP03's program switch to **Program**, then press **Reset**.
2. Open STM32CubeProgrammer and choose **UART**. Select the connected port, baud rate `115200`, even parity, 8 data bits, 1 stop bit and no flow control, then select **Connect**.
3. In **Erasing & Programming**, select your generated `.elf` and enable **Verify programming**.
4. Select **Start Programming** and check for **Download verified successfully**. A completed build alone does not confirm an upload.
5. Disconnect STM32CubeProgrammer, return the AP03 switch to **Run**, then press **Reset**.

### Check serial output

1. Open the serial terminal and select the same port. Close other applications that hold the port.
2. Set it to `115200` baud, 8 data bits, no parity, 1 stop bit and no flow control.
3. Check that `Hello World` appears once per second. If it does not, check the Run switch, Reset, selected port and baud rate.

## Tips

### Import a project

1. Start STM32CubeIDE and choose your workspace.
2. Use **File → Open Projects from File System** (the menu may also mention archives) to select the downloaded project folder, then finish importing.
3. Open **Window → Show View → Project Explorer** if the project list is hidden.
4. Build the imported project, then use the upload procedure above. If migration is requested, retain a copy of the original project and review changes before rebuilding.

For debugging instead of UART uploads, see [Connecting the debugger](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/stm32_debug/).

---

# Blink an LED with STM32CubeIDE

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples-stm/blink/

Use an STM32CubeIDE project to turn the AP03 STM32 MCU LED on and off every second. Covers downloading, importing, building, programming, and checking the result.

## Overview

Turn the LED on the STM32 MCU leaf on and off at one-second intervals.

## Before you start

This example targets **AP03 STM32 MCU**. Complete the [STM32CubeIDE setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/stm32cube_ide/) and prepare to program it with STM32CubeProgrammer. The project uses its included STM32 HAL and drivers; Arduino board packages and libraries are not required.

See [How to run an example](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/reproducing/) for obtaining complete source files and distinguishing build, upload, and execution checks.

## Required leaves

Use the following leaves.

| Type | Name | Quantity |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [AZ62](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az62/) | [Connector Cover](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az62/) | 1 |
| [AZ01](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az01/) | [USB](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az01/) | 1 |
| [AP03](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03/) | [STM32 MCU](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03/) | 1 |
| [AV01](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/power/av01/) | [CR2032](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/power/av01/) | 1 |
| | CR2032 coin cell battery | 1 |
| | M2 × 10 mm screw | 2 |

## Assembly

Assemble the leaves as shown below.

## Source code

1. Obtain and extract the entire [STM32CubeIDE-Sample-Software repository](https://github.com/Leafony/STM32CubeIDE-Sample-Software) using `Code → Download ZIP`. If you use Git, clone the same repository.
2. Locate the extracted [`Blink` folder](https://github.com/Leafony/STM32CubeIDE-Sample-Software/tree/main/Blink). Use the complete project, including `.project`, `.cproject`, `Core`, and `Drivers`. `main.c` alone cannot be built.
3. In STM32CubeIDE, choose `File → Import... → General → Existing Projects into Workspace`. Set `Select root directory` to the `Blink` folder, select the Blink project, and click `Finish`.
4. Choose `Project → Build Project`. Check that it completes without errors and generates `Debug/Blink.elf`.

The download links point to the `main` branch, which may be updated. Use a complete set from the same source instead of mixing newly downloaded files into an older project.

The following four lines inside `while (1)` in [`Core/Src/main.c`](https://github.com/Leafony/STM32CubeIDE-Sample-Software/blob/main/Blink/Core/Src/main.c) control the LED. Line numbers vary by source revision.

```c++
HAL_GPIO_WritePin(GPIOH, GPIO_PIN_3, GPIO_PIN_SET);   // LED on
HAL_Delay(1000);                                    // Wait 1000 ms
HAL_GPIO_WritePin(GPIOH, GPIO_PIN_3, GPIO_PIN_RESET); // LED off
HAL_Delay(1000);                                    // Wait 1000 ms
```

## Execution results

1. Follow the [STM32CubeIDE programming procedure](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/stm32cube_ide/#upload-with-stm32cubeprogrammer) to program the generated `Debug/Blink.elf`. Replace the Hello World filename in that procedure with the Blink file.
2. After confirming successful programming, set the AP03 program switch to Run and press its reset switch.
3. Check that the AP03 LED repeatedly stays **on for one second and off for one second**. A successful build alone does not confirm programming or execution.

If the LED does not blink, check the power supply, ELF file programmed, program switch position, and reset after programming, in that order. If connection fails, see the [FAQ](https://docs.leafony.com/en/faq/).

# Google Sheets IoT

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/avr-mcu/basic/google_sheets_iot/

## Overview

We will create an IoT environment sensor using Leafony Beacon1) and Raspberry Pi, and visualize the sensor data using Google Spreadsheet.

1) Beacon is a facility for acquiring various information including location by receiving radio waves on the ground with a specific device. in the case of Bluetooth Beacon devices, a module equipped with sensors such as temperature and air pressure can be installed at any location to observe the environment of that location.

## What to prepare

* Leafony Basic Kit
* Raspberry Pi (3, 4, zero, etc.)
* PC or smartphone with browser access

# Web Bluetooth IoT

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/avr-mcu/basic/webbluetooth_iot/

This sample is the same as the one introduced in [Basic Kit Getting Started Guide](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/basic/). Let's read the source code to understand how it works.

## Introduction

Leafony is designed to make it easy to develop small, power-saving IoT devices, and each leaf is designed to save power.
Since it runs on battery for a long time, it can be placed in various locations to perform fixed-point observations with sensors.

So how can data such as temperature, humidity, and illumination measured by sensors be collected?
In general, wireless communication such as Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and LoRa is used.
Leafony has a leaf equipped with Bluetooth, one of the most power-efficient wireless communication standards.

The Basic Kit is a kit that makes it easy to develop long battery-powered IoT sensors using the 4-Sensor Leaf, which is equipped with multiple power-saving sensors, and the BLE Leaf, which is equipped with Bluetooth LE (hereinafter referred to as BLE), a power-saving Bluetooth standard.

So what do we need to do in order to receive the BLE sent by Leafony?
There are many different environments for PCs, smartphones, and tablets: PCs running Windows, PCs running MacOS, Android, iPhone, and so on.
In order to use Bluetooth in these environments, it is normal to develop in a programming language tailored to each environment. For PC, you can develop using languages such as C and Python, but for Android and iPhone, you need to use Android Studio, Xcode, etc. to create software in yet another programming language.

How can we easily develop something that is used by many people in many different environments?
In this sample application, one way to do this is to **use a web browser** to communicate via Bluetooth and display the data on the screen.

The languages used are HTML and Java Script. A program written in these two languages will work equally well in any environment on a web browser.

:::note[Points]
* The Web Bluetooth library allows you to write software for Bluetooth connection in a web application.
* If it is a web application, the same source code will work on any device that runs a browser.
* GUIs such as tables and graphs can be easily developed using HTML and CSS.
:::

## What to prepare

* Leafony Basic Kit
* Windows[^1], Mac[^2], or Linux[^3] PC (for development)
* Android[^4], iPhone[^5], iPad[^5] smartphone or tablet (does not have to be for testing)
* Google Chrome (Version 70.0.3526.0 or later)
* Arduino IDE

[^1]: Windows 10 version 1703 or later
[^2]: OS X Yosemite or later
[^3]: Kernel 3.19+ and BlueZ 5.41+ installed.
[^4]: Android 6.0 Marshmallow or later
[^5]: For iPhone or iPad, [WebBLE](https://itunes.apple.com/us/app/webble/id1193531073)(paid) is required.This is because Web Bluetooth is not implemented in the iPhone and iPad versions of Chrome.

## Sample app source code
Please download both in advance.

* [Arduino Sketch](https://github.com/Leafony/Sample-Sketches/tree/master/4-Sensors_BLE)
* [Web Bluetooth App](https://github.com/Leafony/WebBluetooth_for_Leafony_app)

## Leafony Configuration

In this sample, you can try the following leaf configurations.

| Type                                  | Name                                       | Q'ty |
| ------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ | ---- |
| [AZ62](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az62)        | [Connector Cover](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az62)  | 1    |
| [AI01](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai01)            | [4-Sensors](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai01)            | 1    |
| [AZ01](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az01)        | [USB](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az01)              | 1    |
| [AP01](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap01)     | [AVR MCU](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap01)       | 1    |
| [AC02](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac02) | [BLE Sugar](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac02) | 1    |
| [AV01](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/power/av01)         | [CR2032](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/power/av01)            | 1    |

## Assembly

Let's assemble leaves as shown in the figure below.

## Pin assignment
Refer to the figure below for the pin assignment of each leaf.

## Execution method
1. Write [4-Sensors_BLE.ino](https://github.com/Leafony/Sample-Sketches/tree/master/4-Sensors_BLE) in Arduino IDE.
2. Open the downloaded `index.html` of [Web Bluetooth App](https://github.com/Leafony/WebBluetooth_for_Leafony_app) with Google Chrome.
For details, see the [preinstalled AVR demo guide](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/basic/). In the current interface, select **Leafonyに接続する** (Connect to Leafony), choose **Leafony_AC02** in your device's pairing dialog, and pair.

This is an example of the previous interface. The current connection button is **Leafonyに接続する** (Connect to Leafony).

## Sending data

Let's see how to send and receive data with BLE.

### Leafony side

In `4-Sensors_BLE.ino`, around line 1020, we generate the text data to be sent via Bluetooth. Any data can be sent by changing this text.

```cpp title="4-Sensors_BLE.ino"
sendLen = sprintf(sendData, "%04s,%04s,%04s,%04s,%04s,%01s\n", temp, humid, light, tilt, battVolt, pips)
```

In the above, comma-separated data like `<temperature>,<humidity>,<illuminance>,<slope>,<battery voltage>,<dice>` is sent.

The following is the part that actually sends this text data. (Around line 1085)

```cpp title="4-Sensors_BLE.ino"
ble112.ble_cmd_gatt_server_send_characteristic_notification( 1, 0x000C, sendLen, (const uint8 *)sendData );
```

### Web app side

On the web app side, the process for receiving data is written in `leafony.js`.

In line 75 of `leafony.js`, we specify the function to be called when data is received.
Here, the function `handleData()` is called.

```js title="leafony.js"
char.read.addEventListener( 'characteristicvaluechanged', handleData );
```

The `handleData()` function is also described in `leafony.js`.
The data received by the BLE is contained in `event.target.value`.
Once the values are copied into the variable `data`, the received data is decoded in utf-8, the newline code (`\r\n`) is removed, and then the data is made into an array separated by commas `,`.
These data are stored in a variable called `state` with an arbitrary name. (`state.temp`, `state.humid`, etc.)

If the data sent by the Leafony side is changed, it can be decoded by modifying the `handleData()` function.

```js title="leafony.js"
    /**
     * Characteristicの値が変化した時に呼び出される関数
     * @param {*} event
     */
    function handleData( event ) {
        // 受信したデータの文字コードを変換して、カンマでデータを分けている
        // このサンプルではLeafonyは
        // 温度,湿度,傾き,電池の電圧
        // のようにカンマ区切りのテキストを送信している。
        let data = event.target.value;
        let decoder = new TextDecoder( 'utf-8' );
        data = decoder.decode( data );
        data = data.replace( /\r?\n/g, '' );
        data = data.split( ',' );

        state.devn = deviceName;
        state.unin = uniqueName;
        state.temp = data[0];
        state.humd = data[1];
        state.illm = data[2];
        state.tilt = data[3];
        state.batt = data[4];
        state.dice = data[5];
        // ここで updateTable() が実行されている
        onStateChangeCallback( state );

        // 省略
    }
```

## Receiving data

### Web app side

Open **LEDの調整・データの保存** (LED settings and data export) and select **点滅をゆっくりに** (Blink slower) or **点滅を速くする** (Blink faster) to change Leafony's LED blink speed.
The process for when the buttons are pressed is described in the following part of `app.js`.

```js title="app.js"
buttonLedPls.addEventListener ( 'click', function () {

    console.log( 'LED Plus Button Clicked' );
    leafony.sendCommand( 'PLS' );

});
```

`leafony.sendCommand( 'string' );` to send an arbitrary string to Leafony.

### Leafony side

When Leafony receives a string sent from the web app side, the `my_evt_gatt_server_attribute_value()` function in `4-Sensors.ino` will be called.
The decoded string is copied to a variable named `rcv_data` and processed according to the content of the string.

```cpp title="4-Sensors.ino"
void my_evt_gatt_server_attribute_value( const struct ble_msg_gatt_server_attribute_value_evt_t *msg ) {
    uint16 attribute = (uint16)msg -> attribute;
    uint16 offset = 0;
    uint8 value_len = msg -> value.len;

    uint8 value_data[20];
    String rcv_data;
    rcv_data = "";
    for (uint8_t i = 0; i < value_len; i++) {
        rcv_data += (char)(msg -> value.data[i]);
    }

    // 中略

    if( rcv_data.indexOf("SND") == 0 ){
        bBLEsendData = true;
        iToggle = 8;
    } else if( rcv_data.indexOf("STP") == 0 ){
        bBLEsendData = false;
        bLCDchange = true;
        lcd_view_sts = 1;
    } else if(rcv_data.indexOf("PLS") == 0){
      if(iToggle < 16){
        iToggle += 2;
      }
    } else if(rcv_data.indexOf("MNS") == 0){
      if(iToggle > 2){
        iToggle -= 2;
      }
    }
}
```

You can easily send and receive data by modifying the above sections.

## Structure

* Peripheral and Central
* Advertisement
* GATT
* Characteristic

### Web app side

It consists of three files: `index.html`, `app.js`, and `leafony.js`.

The `index.html` is simple enough to place buttons and tables, and load two other javascript files.
`app.js` contains the main processing, such as what happens when a button is pressed.
`leafony.js` describes the specific process of connecting to Leafony using Web Bluetooth.

## Notes on Web Bluetooth

As of June 2020, Web Bluetooth will need to take the following points into account.

* It does not work with Chrome on iPhone.It is available by using a paid application called [WebBLE](https://apps.apple.com/jp/app/webble/id1193531073).
* The development status of Web Bluetooth and supported browsers can be found at [implementation-status.md](https://github.com/WebBluetoothCG/web-bluetooth/blob/master/implementation-status.md).

## Reference
https://qiita.com/s_nkg/items/bdb235388eaeb567b54d
