|              Item              |         Description          |
| :----------------------------- | :--------------------------- |
| Dimension     　               | W24×D20.5×H8.7mm             |

### Power Supply

| Item                   | Description                                |
| :--------------------- | :----------------------------------------- |
| Part number            | TPS61099YFFR                               |
| Battery voltage        | 0.7～3.8V                                  |
| Output voltage         | 3.3V±2%                                    |
| Controlling method     | PWM/PFM Automatic switching control        |
| Maximum output current | 300mA @3.3V to 5V                          |
| Protection circuit     | Over current protection / Thermal shutdown |

### AD Converter

| Item              | Description         |
| :---------------- | :------------------ |

| Resolution        | 8bit                |
| Reference voltage | Vdd(3.3V)           |
| Sample rate       | 188.9kSPS(max)      |
| Interfaces        | I2C (Address: 0x50) |

# AV04A 2V～4.5V

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/power/av04/

## Features

Supply 3.3V power to the leaves from an external battery. You can turn the power on or off with the switch and read the battery voltage from an [MCU (microcontroller)](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#mcu) leaf. The SH connector is intended for two or three dry cells, or Li-Po and Li-ion batteries within the stated voltage range.

This leaf includes a JST SH battery connector, a step-up/down power supply circuit that converts a battery voltage of 2 to 4.5V to 3.3V, and an [I2C](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#i2c)-connected AD converter for measuring battery voltage.

| Controlling method     | PWM/PFM Automatic switching control  |
| Maximum output current | 300mA (when step down)                    |

# AV06 1.8V–5.5V

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/power/av06/

[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/power/av06/av06_f_small.jpg)
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/power/av06/av06_b_small.jpg)
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/power/av06/av06_p_small.jpg)

## Features

Supply 3.3V power at up to 1.0A to other leaves from an external battery. An [MCU (microcontroller)](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#mcu) leaf can also read the battery voltage. The leaf supports two or three dry cells.

It includes a JST PH connector for the battery, a buck-boost power supply circuit that converts a battery voltage of 1.8–5.5V to 3.3V, and an [I2C](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#i2c) analog-to-digital converter for measuring the battery voltage.

## Specifications

### Dimensions

| Item (in progress) | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| Dimension | W23×D20×H5.6mm |

### Power supply

| Item | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| Part number | TPS631010YBGR |
| Battery voltage | 1.8V–5.5V |
| Output voltage | 3.3V±0.3V |
| Maximum output current | 1A |

### Analog-to-digital converter

| Item | Description |
| :--- | :--- |
| Part number | ADC081C027CIMK |
| Resolution | 8bit |
| Reference voltage | Vdd(3.3V) |
| Sample rate | 188.9kSPS (max) |
| Interfaces | I2C (Address: 0x50) |

## Pin assignment

[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/power/av06/av01-4_pinassign.png)

# Processor

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/

Choose a leaf to view its specifications, pin assignments and technical documents.

- [AP01 AVR MCU](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap01/): Run Arduino programs to read connected sensors and control outputs such as LEDs.
- [AP02 ESP32 MCU](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap02/): Run programs and exchange data over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth LE; upload programs over USB.
- [AP03 STM32 MCU](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03/): Read connected sensors and control other leaves with programs running on a 32-bit STM32 MCU.
- [AP05 STM32N6](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap05/): Intended for evaluating image processing and edge AI applications, and for developing STM32N6 firmware.

See also the [leaf reference index](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/) and [I²C address map](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/i2c-address-map/).

---

# AP01 AVR MCU

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap01/

[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap01/ap01a_f_large.jpg)
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap01/ap01a_b_large.jpg)
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap01/ap01a_p_large.jpg)

## Features

Run programs created in Arduino IDE to read connected sensors and control outputs such as LEDs.

This [MCU (microcontroller)](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#mcu) leaf uses the ATmega328P and has 14 digital input/output pins (six support PWM output), six analog input pins, an 8 MHz oscillator, and a reset button. Use a USB leaf for a USB connection or a Shield leaf for ICSP. In Arduino IDE, select the Arduino Pro or Pro Mini board and the ATmega328P (3.3V, 8MHz) processor.

## Specification

| Item              | Description |
| :---------------- | :---------- |
| Part number       | ATmega328P  |
| Operating voltage | 3.3V        |
| Input voltage     | 1.5-5V      |
| Digital I/O       | 14          |
| Analog input      | 6           |
| Flash memory      | 32 KB       |
| SRAM              | 2KB         |
| EEPROM            | 1KB         |
| Clock speed       | 8MHz        |
| Dimension         | W23×D20.5×H4.7mm |

## Block diagram
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap01/ap01a_block.png)

## Pinassign
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap01/ap01_pinassign.png)

## Tips
### About LEDs and switches

[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap01/ap01_tips.jpg)

| Item         | Description                                             |
| :----------- | :------------------------------------------------------ |
| Reset switch | Reset microcontroller or other devices                |
| LED          | Control LED by using pin 13 (Same as Arduino UNO)       |

## Sample App
* [Blink](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/beginner/avr-mcu/basic/blink)

## How to use it with Arduino
In order to use this leaf with Arduino, the board must be configured on the Arduino IDE.
Please refer to [Environment](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/avr/arduino)  for instructions.

* [Component marking](https://github.com/Leafony/HW-Design-Files/blob/master/AP01_AVR_MCU/AP01_AVR_MCU_ComponentMarking.pdf)

# AP02 ESP32 MCU

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap02/

[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap02/ap02a_f_large.jpg)
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap02/ap02a_b_large.jpg)
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap02/ap02a_p_large.jpg)

## Features

Use Arduino IDE to create programs that read connected sensors and send or receive data over Wi-Fi or [BLE](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#ble). Connect this [MCU (microcontroller)](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#mcu) leaf to a PC over USB to upload programs and check their operation with the serial monitor.

It uses Espressif Systems' ESP32-WROOM-32 module with an Xtensa Dual-Core 32-bit LX6 processor and certified Wi-Fi and BLE. Radio certifications include FCC, CE-RED, IC, TELEC, KCC, SRRC, and NCC (Espressif Systems Data Sheet V2.9). USB power can also supply VBUS (5V) to other leaves.

## Specification

| Item                | Description                                 |
| :------------------ | :------------------------------------------ |
| Part number         | ESP32-WROOM-32                              |
| SoC                 | ESP32-D0WDQ6 (CPU:Xtensa LX6)               |
| Operating voltage   | 3.3V                                        |
| Input voltage       | 2.2-3.6V                                    |
| Digital I/O         | 14                                          |
| Analog input        | 6                                           |
| TouchSensor I/F     | 6                                           |
| Flash Memory        | 4 MB                                        |
| SRAM                | 520 KB                                      |
| Clock frequency     | 80M-240MHz                                  |
| Wi-Fi protocols     | IEEE 802.11b/g/n                            |
| Bluetooth protocols | Bluetooth v4.2 BR/EDR and BLE specification |
| RF certification    | FCC/CE-RED/IC/TELEC/KCC/SRRC/NCC            |
| Dimension           | W39.1×D32.7×H5.4mm    　　　　　　　　　　　  |

## Block diagram
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap02/ap02a_block.png)

## Pinassign
[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap02/ap02_pinassign.png)

## Tips
### About LEDs and switches

[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap02/ap02_tips.jpg)

| Item             | Description                                                                                                        |
| :--------------- | :----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| LED RX           | FT232RQ controlled LED / Flashes on UART TX data transmission.                                                     |
| LED TX           | FT232RQ controlled LED / Flashes on UART RX data transmission.                                                     |
| Reset switch     | Resets the ESP32 and other devices.                                                                                |
| Boot mode switch | Switch to change to boot mode.Press and hold the boot mode switch while writing a sketch.                          |
| micro USB        | It is used for writing a sketch to the MCU and serial monitoring by connecting a PC.This also converts USB’s VBUS(5V) to 3.3V by using step-down power circuit and provide VBUS and 3.3V to each leaf. |
| Antenna          | This is a shared antenna for Bluetooth LE and Wi-Fi.  |

* [ESP32 googlesheets](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/esp32-mcu/esp32/esp32_googlesheets_1)

## How to use it with Arduino
In order to use this leaf with Arduino, the board must be configured on the Arduino IDE.
Please refer to [Environment](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/esp32/arduino)  for instructions.

# AP03 STM32 MCU: Arduino-Compatible Microcontroller Leaf

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03/

Find Leafony AP03 STM32L452REI6 specifications, pin assignments, schematics and Arduino board settings, with sensor-reading and BLE beacon examples.

## Features

Run programs that read connected sensors and control other leaves based on their readings. Development with Arduino IDE is supported.

This 32-bit [MCU (microcontroller)](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#mcu) leaf uses STMicroelectronics' STM32L452RE series with an Arm Cortex-M4 core and FPU. Use a USB leaf for a USB connection or a Shield leaf for SWD.

# AP03B STM32 MCU

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03b/

AP03B v1.1 (STM32L452RET6) specifications, Leafony Bus pinout, PG and reset controls, and AP03-compatible board settings.

## Features

AP03B v1.1 is an [MCU (microcontroller)](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#mcu) leaf that reads sensors and controls communication leaves and other modules. It uses the STM32L452RET6 and has the same Leafony Bus pin assignments as the [AP03 STM32 MCU](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03/).

It connects to other leaves through the Leafony Bus and operates from 3.3V. The board includes a PG switch for BOOT0, a reset switch, and an LED indicating the BOOT0 state.

## Specifications

| Item | Description |
| --- | --- |
| MCU | STMicroelectronics STM32L452RET6 (LQFP64, 10 × 10 mm, 0.5 mm pitch) |
| CPU | Arm Cortex-M4 with FPU |
| Maximum clock | 80 MHz (MCU specification) |
| Flash memory | 512 KB |
| SRAM | 160 KB |
| Power | Leafony Bus 3.3V / GND |
| Low-speed external clock | 32.768 kHz crystal (X1) |
| Main bus signals | D0–D13, A0–A5, SDA / SCL, SWDIO / SWCLK, RESET |
| Bus contacts | 29 contacts on each side (CN1) |
| Board dimensions | 23 × 20 mm (maximum PCB outline) |
| Board thickness / layers | 0.8 mm, 4 layers (excluding component height) |
| Design revision | v1.1, November 20, 2026 |

See [STMicroelectronics product information](https://www.st.com/en/microcontrollers-microprocessors/stm32l452re.html) for CPU and memory specifications. The actual clock depends on the firmware configuration.

All components are mounted on the top side. The second layer (L2) is a dedicated ground plane. The top (L1), inner (L3) and bottom (L4) layers also have ground pours. Plated through vias sit outside the pads and have a 0.45 mm diameter and a 0.25 mm drill.

## Power and external connections

Supply the Leafony Bus 3.3V terminal from a power leaf or other suitable source. **The VBUS terminal is not connected to the AP03B circuitry.**

R2 pulls SDA up to 3.3V, and R1 does the same for SCL. Both resistors are 10 kΩ. Before connecting external devices, check the [Leafony Bus specification](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leafony-bus/) and the other device's power and signal voltages.

AREF connection resistor R5 is DNP (not populated), so the bus AREF terminal is not connected to the MCU's analog supply/reference circuit in the standard configuration.

## Pin connections

Front and back contacts with the same number (such as F1 / B1) carry the same signal. The Port columns show MCU port names, which differ from the pin numbers used in Arduino sketches.

[](https://docs.leafony.com/leaf/processor/ap03b/ap03b-pinout-en.svg)

Click the diagram to enlarge it. Select AP03B in the [Pin Assignment Editor](https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/pinout-editor/) to edit the diagram and save it as PNG or SVG.

Connections are based on the [Leafony Bus schematic](https://github.com/leafony/ap03b-stm32/blob/main/kicad/ap03b-stm32/leafony_bus.kicad_sch) and [MCU schematic](https://github.com/leafony/ap03b-stm32/blob/main/kicad/ap03b-stm32/stm32.kicad_sch). R5, R7, R12 and R14 are not populated.

## Switches and LED

| Component | Marking or location | Function |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SW1 | PG | Selects BOOT0 high / low. |
| SW2 | RST marking on the underside | Connects RESET to GND when pressed. |
| D1 | Lower right on the top side, with the bus contacts at the top | Lights when BOOT0 is high. The LED faces outward at the lower edge so you can see it from the side of a stack. |

The LED indicates the BOOT0 state, not program execution or a successful upload.

## Development environment

AP03B v1.1 supports the existing AP03 board definition. In the Arduino IDE, when using the STM32duino “STM32 MCU based boards” package, select **Generic STM32L4 series** as the board and **Leafony AP03** as the board part number. For a new PlatformIO project, set `board = leafony_ap03` in `platformio.ini`. [STM32duino board definitions](https://github.com/stm32duino/Arduino_Core_STM32/blob/main/boards.txt) · [PlatformIO AP03 settings](https://docs.platformio.org/en/latest/boards/ststm32/leafony_ap03.html)

For the Cat-M1 Kit's AP03B + AI05 + AC09 configuration, use the [Google Sheets temperature and humidity sample](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/ac09_google_sheets/). Open `platformio/google_sheets` in the AC09 development repository and select the PlatformIO environment `leafony_ap03b`. Follow the sample instructions for uploading through the AZ01C USB-C leaf and operating PG/RST.

The following documentation covers shared STM32 MCU development tools:

- [STM32 MCU start guide](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/stm32/)
- [Arduino IDE setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/arduino_ide/)
- [PlatformIO setup](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/platformio/)
- [Debugger connection](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/stm32_debug/)

# Leafony Bus Specifications and Connections

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/leafony-bus/

Learn the names of the 29 Leafony Bus contacts, the roles of 3.3V and VBUS, MCU-specific pin functions, and the power, signal, and size requirements to check.

The Leafony Bus is the common contact area that connects power and signals between stacked leaves. Place an [AZ61 Connector](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az61/) between leaves and secure them with screws to make the connection.

This page explains contact names and roles. Available functions, voltages, and currents depend on the connected leaves. When choosing a configuration, also read [Combining Leaves and Choosing a Power Supply](https://docs.leafony.com/en/guides/combining-leaves/).

## Contact Area Dimensions

The common contact area measures **20 × 5.5 mm**, the board is **0.8 mm** thick, and the contacts are gold plated. These dimensions do not describe the entire leaf or its height including components. Check each leaf's outline and the height of adjacent components separately.

For board layout data, see [AX02 29pin](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/extension/ax02/). Board design templates are available under [Custom Leaf Development](https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/).

## Names and Roles of the 29 Contacts

The table below lists the common Leafony Bus contact names. Numeric signal names in each leaf's pin assignment diagram, such as `8`, are written as `D8` here. Distinguish contact numbers such as `F1`, bus signal names such as `D8`, and MCU port names such as `PA9`.

| Contact number | Bus signal name | Role and checks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 3V3 / 3.3V | 3.3V power line. Check which leaf supplies or receives power and the current required |
| 2 | SWDIO | SWD data signal. Check the selected MCU leaf's pin assignment for its connection |
| 3 | VBUS | Line associated with USB power. Check its connection and use on each leaf |
| 4 | AREF | Analog reference voltage connection; may be unconnected |
| 5 | RESET | Reset signal |
| 6 | A0 | Analog input or other function. Check the MCU assignment |
| 7 | D6 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 8 | A1 | Analog input or other function |
| 9 | D7 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 10 | A2 | Analog input or other function |
| 11 | D8 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 12 | A3 | Analog input or other function |
| 13 | D9 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 14 | A4 | Analog input or other function |
| 15 | D10 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 16 | A5 | Analog input or other function |
| 17 | D11 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 18 | D0 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 19 | D12 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 20 | D1 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 21 | D13 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 22 | D2 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 23 | SDA | I2C data |
| 24 | D3 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 25 | SCL | I2C clock |
| 26 | D4 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 27 | GND | Power and signal reference |
| 28 | D5 | Digital I/O or peripheral function |
| 29 | SWCLK | SWD clock signal. Check the selected MCU leaf's pin assignment for its connection |

Check each leaf's pin assignment diagram for contact positions and front/back orientation. This table does not specify absolute maximum electrical ratings or the internal connections of every leaf.

## Functions That Depend on the MCU

The MCU port, UART/SPI/PWM functions, and Arduino pin number associated with a bus signal can differ between boards. Check the selected board definition against the pin assignments in your example.

For example, the [AP03 pin assignment diagram](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03/) connects D8 to PA9 and D9 to PA10 for UART use. On [AP03B](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03b/), a switch between D9 and PA10 disconnects them when BOOT0 is High. AP03B's AREF is also unconnected to the MCU in its standard assembly. Matching contact names do not mean that swapping a leaf preserves the same behavior.

## Checking Power and Signals

- **Distinguish 3.3V from VBUS.** Check the power supplied by the USB leaf and battery leaf, and the power received by each connected leaf. Do not treat a power input voltage range as the allowable voltage for GPIO (general-purpose input/output) pins.
- **Check multiple power sources.** Before connecting USB and a battery together, check reverse-current protection and simultaneous supply conditions for each power leaf. [AZ01C USB-C](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/others/az01c/) explains its different power states.
- **Compare shared signal assignments.** Check inputs, outputs, UART/SPI pins, reset signals, and interrupt connections on each leaf. Whether multiple outputs can share a line depends on their circuits and control methods.
- **Check I2C addresses and pull-ups.** Use the [I2C Address Map](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/i2c-address-map/) to compare devices sharing SDA/SCL. Check the pull-up resistors on each MCU and sensor leaf.

## Related Guides

- [Combining Leaves and Choosing a Power Supply](https://docs.leafony.com/en/guides/combining-leaves/): checks before selecting a configuration
- [Assembling and Replacing Leaves](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/assembly/): connectors, spacers, and fastening parts
- [Pin Assignment Editor](https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/pinout-editor/): compare pin usage across leaves
- [Custom Leaf Development](https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/): CAD templates and design documents

# Low-Power IoT Sensor Design and Battery Runtime Calculations

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/lowpower/

Estimate power, average current and battery runtime for Leafony IoT sensors, use STM32 sleep modes and learn how to measure energy use on your device.

Leafony is designed for compact, battery-powered systems. Runtime depends on the complete circuit, its program and its power supply. Start by identifying where energy is spent, then measure the assembled device.

## Thinking about low-power design

When building a circuit, consider both its power consumption and whether the intended supply can provide enough power. USB supplies and AC adapters can often supply a few watts for long periods. A battery-powered device also needs to make its limited stored energy last.

A larger battery can extend runtime, but a small device such as a wristwatch needs a small battery. Small changes in consumption can then have a large effect on runtime. For a compact system such as Leafony, low-power design is an important part of its performance.

## Power and energy

For a constant voltage and current, power is `P = V × I`. One watt is one volt times one ampere. Energy is power multiplied by time: `1 Wh = 1 W × 1 h`.

Measure current at the battery to calculate the complete circuit's power. Individual components draw different currents, and their current can change with their operating state. A resistor's current is determined by the applied voltage and resistance, whereas an IC's internal activity affects its current. Battery voltage can also change during use.

ICs contain analog or digital circuits. In digital circuits such as CPUs, logic gates are commonly built from MOSFETs. In the simplified example below, a NOT gate draws a large pulse of current when its input changes. A 0 V input (LOW) produces a 5 V output (HIGH); when the input rises to 5 V, the output falls toward 0 V.

The top trace shows the input transition, the middle trace shows the output response, and the bottom trace shows the current pulse. Here, the current while the input remains unchanged is called leakage current, and the current associated with switching is called dynamic current. This example ignores leakage to focus on switching power.

The following example applies a clock of frequency `f` to a NOT gate. Wiring and the inputs of subsequent gates contribute parasitic load capacitance at its output. For switching in a digital circuit, a simplified model is:

```text
P = α * C * V^2 * f
```

Here P is average switching power, C is load capacitance, V is supply voltage, f is clock frequency, and α is the number of charging events per clock cycle. This excludes leakage and short-circuit current. Under these assumptions, power is proportional to clock frequency. A faster CPU clock can increase processing speed as well as power consumption.

## Identify the loads

Knowing that power depends on frequency does not tell us the number of logic gates or the capacitance inside an IC. We can estimate its consumption from the manufacturer's data sheet without knowing every detail of its internal circuit.

| Leaf | Main device | Conditions to compare |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [AP01 AVR MCU](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap01/) | ATmega328P | Clock frequency, active and sleep states, enabled peripherals |
| [AP03 STM32 MCU](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03/) | STM32L452REI6 | 16 / 80 MHz, run / sleep / stop, RTC and other peripherals |
| [AI01 4-Sensors](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai01/) | HTS221TR, OPT3001, LIS2DHTR | Measurement interval, continuous / single measurement / power-down |
| [AC02 BLE Sugar](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac02/) | BGM11S22F256GA-V2 | Transmit power, interval, connection / beacon / sleep |

Follow the specifications and schematic links in each reference page, then consult the component data sheets at the actual supply voltage, temperature and operating mode. This table identifies what to investigate; it is not a table of measured current. Include LEDs, resistors and power converters when measuring a complete leaf.

Record the leaf model and revision, firmware, supply voltage, instrument, temperature, mode, measurement interval and average current. Distinguish typical values from maximum values, and data-sheet values from measurements.

## Estimate battery runtime

Battery charge capacity is measured in ampere-hours: `1 Ah = 1 A × 1 h`. Multiply by nominal voltage to estimate stored energy.

One ampere-hour is the charge needed to supply one ampere for one hour. It does not specify voltage: a 1 Ah battery at 1.5 V stores a different amount of energy from one at 3 V. Watt-hours let us compare batteries at different voltages, although changing battery voltage makes an exact energy calculation more complex.

The following are assumed values for arithmetic examples, not specifications for all products:

| Example battery | Assumed nominal voltage and capacity | Nominal energy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CR2032 coin cell | 3.0 V, 220 mAh | 660 mWh |
| AA nickel-metal hydride cell | 1.2 V, 2,000 mAh | 2,400 mWh |
| Lithium-ion cell | 3.7 V, 3,000 mAh | 11,100 mWh |

The CR2032 in this example stores about 28% of the energy of the AA cell. Actual capacity depends on the product, temperature and discharge conditions; check the data sheet for the battery you plan to use.

:::caution[Idealized calculation]
These examples assume 100% power conversion efficiency and access to the entire nominal battery capacity. They exclude self-discharge, voltage sag, temperature, internal resistance and cutoff voltage. In particular, they do not imply that a CR2032 can supply a 100 mA load. Check the current capability of the battery and power leaf separately.
:::

A constant 3.3 V, 100 mA load consumes 330 mW. Under the assumptions above, a 660 mWh battery gives `660 / 330 = 2 h`; a 2,400 mWh battery gives approximately `7.3 h`.

### A load that sleeps between measurements

Assume a circuit draws 100 mA for one minute each hour and 1 mA for the remaining 59 minutes, all at 3.3 V.

```text
Average current = 100 mA × 1/60 + 1 mA × 59/60 = 2.65 mA
Average power = 3.3 V × 2.65 mA = 8.745 mW
Energy used in one hour = 8.745 mWh
Ideal runtime = 660 mWh / 8.745 mW ≈ 75.5 h ≈ 3.14 days
```

This is a theoretical example, not a measured Leafony runtime.

## Reduce energy use

The following techniques are used in the [STM32 Logger Beacon sample](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/stm32_logger_ble_beacon/).

### Lower the clock frequency when possible

The CPU is a major digital circuit in a Leafony system. The STM32 leaf defaults to 80 MHz, and Leafony provides both 80 MHz and 16 MHz board options. Selecting a lower clock trades processing performance for lower switching power.

In Arduino IDE, open **Tools → Board part number → Leafony STM32 MCU** and select the required frequency. See the [Arduino setup guide](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/arduino_ide/) for the board package settings.

Choose a frequency based on whether the application needs fast computation or prioritizes low-power operation. Another approach is to get the sketch working at a higher frequency, then reduce the frequency and test its behavior at each available setting.

### Put unused circuits to sleep or power them down

Each component uses energy, even if it is temporarily unnecessary. For example, a system can read the four measurements from 4-Sensors and then send them through a BLE leaf. The sensor ICs are not needed during BLE transmission, so putting them into sleep modes after reading reduces consumption. This matters especially when running from a coin cell.

The STM32 chip also contains multiple internal circuits whose sleep states can be controlled separately to reduce consumption.

### Wake the CPU with interrupts

When the circuit only needs to react to external events, use the CPU's interrupt functions to wake it from sleep when needed.

## Measure and verify

1. Record the leaves, firmware, battery and voltage.
2. Measure current on the battery side over a complete cycle, including startup, sensing, radio transmission and sleep. Check that the instrument's voltage drop does not affect operation.
3. Average current over time. If voltage changes, average the product of voltage and current to obtain average power.
4. Change one setting at a time and compare with the estimate.
5. Verify runtime using the intended battery and operating temperature.

For choosing a measurement location, connecting AX05B and a current meter, and comparing complete active/sleep cycles, see [Measure Current and Reduce Power Consumption](https://docs.leafony.com/en/guides/measuring-power/).

# About Leafony: A Compact, Low-Power IoT Development Platform

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/overview/

Build IoT prototypes with small sensor, wireless and display boards. Learn about Leafony, choose a kit, set up development tools and try sample applications.

## What is Leafony?

Leafony is an IoT development platform for prototyping devices by stacking small circuit boards called leaves. Choose the functions you need to measure temperature and humidity, send data, or provide display and sound output.

Leafony is currently manufactured and sold by [mitdir Inc.](https://mitdir.jp/). Products are available from the [Leafony Shop](https://shop.leafony.com/).

### How leaves work together

Combine sensor, communication and display leaves with an [MCU (microcontroller)](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#mcu) and a power supply. Check that the power, pins and software support your chosen setup. Battery runtime also depends on the leaves and program you use.

[Learn how to combine leaves and choose a power supply](https://docs.leafony.com/en/guides/combining-leaves/)

### Use cases

Measure temperature and humidity, then send the readings to a spreadsheet over a cellular network.

Choose sensor, communication and display leaves to test the functions you need before designing a custom board.

Use a kit and sample code to display sensor readings or send them wirelessly.

## Get started

- Before buying: [Choose a kit](https://docs.leafony.com/en/products/)
- Already have a kit: [Run the preinstalled demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/)
- Ready to run your own program: [Set up your development environment](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/)
- Looking for something to build: [Explore sample applications](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/)

If you need help, [browse common questions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/) or [ask a question](https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/ask/).

## Introduction materials

See the leaf roles and overall configuration on one page.

- [Leafony overview flyer (Japanese, A4 PDF)](https://docs.leafony.com/downloads/leafony-overview-a4-ja.pdf)
- [View the flyer as an image (Japanese)](https://docs.leafony.com/downloads/leafony-overview-a4-ja.png)

### Explore application examples

The [Nanocon Handbook, 7th edition (May 2026, Japanese PDF)](https://www.mcpc-jp.org/pdf/nanoconhandbook7han_20260501.pdf), published by MCPC, introduces Leafony and award-winning contest projects.

### Media coverage and features

Explore articles about Leafony and the Trillion-Node Study Group in the [Leafony Shop media coverage list (Japanese)](https://shop.leafony.com/pages/media).

## Development background

Development history and the Leafony name

Leafony grew out of the Trillion-Node Engine research and development project supported by Japan's New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization (NEDO). It was publicly released in 2019. Read the [original announcement from the University of Tokyo (Japanese PDF)](https://www.t.u-tokyo.ac.jp/shared/press/data/setnws_201910181119504557001333_369954.pdf) for the development background.

The name combines “Leaf” and “Symphony”: individual leaves work together to create something new.

The [Trillion-Node Study Group (Japanese)](https://trillion-node.org/) provides a forum for sharing Leafony technology and applications. For the current business arrangements, see the [Leafony Shop's operator change announcement (Japanese)](https://shop.leafony.com/blogs/news/260307).

[Licensing and trademarks](https://docs.leafony.com/en/license/)

# Home-made leaf development

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/

CAD templates, pin assignments, a pin assignment editor, and the I2C address map for designing your own leaf

This page brings together resources for designing your own leaf. Use a CAD template for the board layout, and check the pin assignments and I2C addresses of the leaves you plan to combine.

## CAD Templates

The templates include the leaf outline, Leafony bus footprint, and design rules. Each page provides a download link and instructions.

- [KiCad Template Project](https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/kicad/)
- [CR-8000 Design Force Template Design Data](https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/cr-8000_design_force/)

## Pin Assignments

Leaf pin assignments are collected in the [pin assignment resources (GitHub: Leafony/Documents)](https://github.com/Leafony/Documents/tree/main/Leaf-pinassign). When designing your circuit, check the pins and signals used by the leaves you plan to combine.

Use the [Pin Assignment Editor](https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/pinout-editor/) to create a diagram for one leaf or a table comparing pin usage across multiple leaves, then save it as a PNG or SVG image.

## I2C Address Map

The [I2C Address Map](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/i2c-address-map/) lists the addresses of I2C devices on each leaf. If you use I2C devices on your own leaf, choose addresses that do not overlap with addresses already in use or reserved addresses.

# CR-8000 Design Force Template Design Data

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/cr-8000_design_force/

## Overview
The Leafony template design data for the CR-8000 Design Force makes leaf board design easy. The template design data contains the following items.
* 2cm x 2cm Leaf outline
* Leafony bus footprint
* Other Parts Footprint
* Design rule

## Download
You can download the template design data from the link below.

[GitHub - Leafony/cad-template](https://github.com/Leafony/cad-template)

## Development Environment
* CR-8000 Design Force 2020 or later

## Usage
1.	Start the CR-8000 Design Force.
2.	`File -> Open -> Design Data`.
3.	Select the template design data you downloaded and click `Open`.

# KiCad Template Project

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/kicad/

How to register the template, configure libraries, and start designing a Leafony expansion leaf with KiCad 10.0.x

## Overview

The Leafony template for KiCad lets you start designing an expansion leaf with the Leafony bus contacts and board outline already configured. It includes a schematic, PCB, dedicated symbol and footprint libraries, layer configuration, and design rules.

The setup and usage instructions on this page are based on the [KiCad template README on GitHub (Japanese)](https://github.com/leafony/cad-template/blob/main/KiCad/README.md).

## Development environment

- [KiCad 10.0.x](https://www.kicad.org/download/)
- KiCad's standard symbol and footprint libraries

When starting KiCad for the first time, choose the option to use its standard libraries. If your system provides the libraries as separate packages, as on some Linux distributions, install those packages as well. Power symbols in the schematic use the standard `power` library.

## Download

On [GitHub - leafony/cad-template](https://github.com/leafony/cad-template), select **Code → Download ZIP** and extract the archive. If you use Git, you can download the repository with this command:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/leafony/cad-template.git
```

Download the entire folder, since the project also needs its libraries and other referenced files. In the paths below, replace `cad-template` with the actual folder where you cloned the repository or extracted the ZIP archive.

### Main files

The following files and folders are inside `cad-template/KiCad/Leafony_Template/`.

| Path | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `Leafony_Template.kicad_pro` | Project settings, design rules, and net classes |
| `Leafony_Template.kicad_sch` | Schematic with the Leafony bus, power connections, and signal labels |
| `Leafony_Template.kicad_pcb` | PCB with the board outline, contacts, vias, and copper zone keepouts |
| `lib/Leafony.kicad_sym` | `Leafony Bus` symbol |
| `lib/Leafony.pretty/` | `CN_F29_B29` footprint |
| `sym-lib-table` | Project-specific symbol library table; empty as distributed |
| `fp-lib-table` | Project-specific footprint library table; `Leafony` is already registered |
| `meta/` | Template name, description, icon, and preview image |

Register `lib/Leafony.kicad_sym` as the symbol library, rather than the legacy files `leafony_template-cache.lib`, `lib/Leafony.dcm`, or `lib/Leafony.bak`. The `.kicad_prl` and `fp-info-cache` files contain personal settings and cached data; they are not libraries to register.

## Usage

### Register the user template

1. Launch the KiCad project manager.
2. Open **Preferences → Configure Paths…**. Menu names may vary with your OS and display language.
3. Set `KICAD_USER_TEMPLATE_DIR` to the **absolute path of the `KiCad` folder** in the downloaded repository.
4. Save the settings. If the template does not appear in the list, restart KiCad.

| OS | Example setting |
| --- | --- |
| Windows | `C:/Users/your-name/Documents/cad-template/KiCad` |
| macOS | `/Users/your-name/Documents/cad-template/KiCad` |
| Linux | `/home/your-name/cad-template/KiCad` |

This variable must point to the parent folder containing `Leafony_Template`. Check that `Leafony_Template/meta/info.html` exists under the configured folder.

If you already use another user template folder, you can keep that setting and copy the entire `Leafony_Template` folder into it.

### Create a new project

1. In the project manager, select **File → New Project…**.
2. Select **Leafony Leaf** from the template list. Filter the list to user templates if needed.
3. Click **OK**, then choose a working folder and a new project name, such as `my_leaf`.
4. Open the generated `my_leaf.kicad_pro`, then launch the schematic and PCB editors from the project manager.

The template files are copied into the new project, and the main files are renamed to match the project name. The `lib` folder and library tables are also copied. Save the new project in a different location from the original template folder.

To inspect the template, you can open `Leafony_Template/Leafony_Template.kicad_pro` directly. To design your own leaf, edit the newly created project.

### Configure the symbol library

The template's `sym-lib-table`, copied into the new project, is empty as distributed. Placed symbols are also stored in the schematic, but you must register the library to add or reference symbols from it.

1. Open the schematic editor from the project manager.
2. Open **Preferences → Manage Symbol Libraries…**.
3. Select **Project Specific Libraries**.
4. Use the option to add an existing library and select `lib/Leafony.kicad_sym` inside your new project.
5. Set the entries to the following values, enable the library, and save.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Nickname | `Leafony` |
| Library path | `${KIPRJMOD}/lib/Leafony.kicad_sym` |
| Library format | `KiCad` |

`${KIPRJMOD}` is the current project folder, set automatically by KiCad. You do not need to add or change it in the path settings.

Check that `Leafony:Leafony Bus` appears in the symbol chooser. If you are using the existing `CN1`, you do not need to place another symbol just to check the library.

### Check the footprint library

The footprint library is already registered in `fp-lib-table`, so no additional setup is normally needed. In the PCB editor, open **Preferences → Manage Footprint Libraries…** and check the project-specific libraries.

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Nickname | `Leafony` |
| Library path | `${KIPRJMOD}/lib/Leafony.pretty` |
| Library format | `KiCad` |

The library is configured correctly if `Leafony:CN_F29_B29` appears. If you register it again, select the `Leafony.pretty` folder, not an individual `.kicad_mod` file.

When moving or sharing the project with another PC, copy the entire project, including the `lib` folder and library tables, to preserve the relative references using `${KIPRJMOD}`.

## Start designing

### Template defaults

The values below are the settings in the included files. Check the layer configuration, manufacturing constraints, and net classes in **Board Setup**, and compare them with your manufacturer's requirements.

| Item | Default value |
| --- | --- |
| Board outline | Maximum `Edge.Cuts` dimensions: 23 × 20 mm. The connector side is 20 mm wide, with extensions on both sides of the board |
| Copper layers | 4 layers: `F.Cu` / `In1.Cu` / `In2.Cu` / `B.Cu` |
| Board thickness | 0.8 mm |
| Bus contacts | `CN1`, with 29 contacts on each side (`F1`–`F29` and `B1`–`B29`) |
| Mounting holes | Two non-plated holes, 2.05 mm in diameter |
| Minimum track width and minimum clearance | 0.1016 mm |
| Track width for the `Default` net class | 0.127 mm |
| Via diameter / drill diameter for the `Default` net class | 0.56 mm / 0.30 mm |

Copper zone keepouts are configured around the connector. Use the PCB data as the reference for the actual board outline, contact positions, and hole positions.

### Edit the schematic and PCB

1. Check the pin assignments of the leaves you will use, then add components and wiring to the schematic. Verify the Leafony bus contact numbers and existing signal names as you connect them.
2. Assign footprints to the added components and run the schematic's electrical rules check (ERC).
3. Select **Tools → Update PCB from Schematic…** to apply the changes to the PCB.
4. Check the contact and mounting hole positions, as well as possible component interference with other leaves, then place the components and route the board.
5. Refill the copper zones and run the design rules check (DRC) to check for unconnected items and manufacturing rule violations.
6. Export the Gerber and drill files, and check them against your manufacturer's requirements.

See the [Custom Leaf Development](https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/) resources for pin assignments and I2C addresses.

## Troubleshooting

| Symptom | What to check |
| --- | --- |
| `Leafony Leaf` does not appear in the template list | Check that `KICAD_USER_TEMPLATE_DIR` points to the parent folder of `Leafony_Template`, with `Leafony_Template/meta/info.html` underneath it. Reopen the list or restart KiCad. |
| KiCad reports that the file format is too new | Check that you are opening the files with KiCad 10.0.x. |
| The `Leafony` symbol library cannot be found | Register `Leafony` in the new project's symbol library table. It is not registered in the distributed table. |
| `Leafony:CN_F29_B29` cannot be found | Check that the project contains `lib/Leafony.pretty` and `fp-lib-table`, and that the nickname and path match the settings above. |
| Standard symbols such as `power` cannot be found | Check that KiCad's standard libraries are installed and enabled in the global library table. |
| Libraries cannot be found after moving to another PC | Copy the `lib` folder as well, and check that library paths use `${KIPRJMOD}` instead of absolute paths from the original PC. |

## License

The template is released under the MIT license.

# Pin Assignment Editor

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/pcb/pinout-editor/

Create Leafony pin assignment diagrams and tables comparing pin usage across leaves, then download them as PNG or SVG images.

Create a pin assignment diagram for one leaf or a table comparing pin usage across multiple leaves. Edit the port names and signals, then download your diagram as a PNG or SVG image.

## How to use

1. Select a leaf or add one from a template. You can compare up to eight leaves and remove a leaf with its "×" button. For a custom leaf, start with a blank template.
2. Edit the leaf name and each pin's port name, signal name, and category. Switch between "Single leaf" and "Leaf comparison" to check the result.
3. Save the image as PNG or SVG. To continue editing later, save your editing data as JSON.

On your first visit, the editor starts with AP03B, AI05, AC09, AV06, and AZ01C. Your edits are saved automatically in your current browser, and your saved configuration opens on your next visit. To continue on another device, load the JSON file you saved.

For templates marked "Pins not entered," check the technical documentation before entering pin assignments. AC05 uses dedicated contacts that differ from the standard 29-pin interface and is outside the scope of this tool.

This tool draws the pin information you enter. It does not automatically determine whether leaves can be connected together. When designing a circuit, check pin voltages and connection requirements in the [technical documentation for each leaf](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/).

# Privacy and analytics

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/privacy/

How Leafony documentation uses Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity.

This site uses Google Analytics to understand site traffic and improve its documentation.

Google Analytics uses cookies and similar technologies to collect information about pages viewed, referring pages, browsers and devices, and interactions such as scrolling and link clicks. This information is sent to Google. We use the resulting reports to understand visitor numbers, popular pages, and traffic sources.

For information about how Google handles this data, see the [Google Privacy Policy](https://policies.google.com/privacy?hl=en) and [How Google uses information from sites or apps that use our services](https://policies.google.com/technologies/partner-sites?hl=en).

To disable the use of data by Google Analytics, you can install the [Google Analytics Opt-out Browser Add-on](https://tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout?hl=en) in a supported browser. See the linked page for compatibility and setup instructions.

## Microsoft Clarity

We use Microsoft Clarity to improve the readability and usability of these docs. On eligible pages, measurement starts without cookies by default. Page visits, clicks, scrolling, and browser and device information are sent to Microsoft and help us understand usage through heatmaps and similar reports. Without cookies, we cannot connect activity across pages or recognize returning visitors as part of the same journey.

Use “Analytics settings” at the bottom of each page to choose “Measure without cookies”, “Allow cookies for analytics”, or “Stop collection”. Allowing cookies enables Clarity cookies for session recordings and journeys across pages. “Stop collection” stops further Clarity collection; it does not delete information already sent. Your choice is saved in this browser and can be changed at any time. Set it separately on other browsers or devices. Previously saved choices to stop collection remain in effect.

We apply strict masking to text and inputs. Clarity does not load on contact, question-form, or privacy pages, or URLs containing query parameters. Recording stops on the current page when you start using an input, such as search. Clarity also stays off when your browser enables Do Not Track (DNT) or Global Privacy Control (GPC), or when your settings cannot be saved or read.

Microsoft processes the information it receives to provide Clarity and for purposes such as improving its products and services, in accordance with its privacy statement and Clarity terms. We always send advertising consent as denied, disabling data sharing from Clarity to Microsoft Ads. This setting does not stop all processing by Microsoft, including providing and improving Clarity. For more information, see the [Microsoft Privacy Statement](https://privacy.microsoft.com/en-us/privacystatement) and [Clarity Terms of Use](https://clarity.microsoft.com/terms).

These settings apply to Clarity. For Google Analytics settings, see the section above.

## Information collected through the question form

We use your email address, question, tried steps, hardware and development environment, publication preference, and consent record to review and answer questions and improve support. Submissions are stored on an access-restricted server and are not published automatically. We retain them only for as long as needed for handling and administration.

Even with publication permission, we remove email addresses and personal or confidential information before staff review and edit the question and answer for publication. Questions marked for private replies only are not published.

To handle your question, we share its title, text, reply email address, hardware and development environment, tried steps, reference number, and publication preference in a private Slack channel accessible only to support staff. Sharing within the support team is separate from permission to publish in the public Q&A. Questions marked for private replies only are still shared with support staff, but are not published publicly. For questions submitted under the earlier notice that excluded text and contact details from Slack, we keep that handling unchanged.

We use Cloudflare Turnstile to prevent spam; Cloudflare processes browser and connection information. See [Cloudflare’s privacy policy](https://www.cloudflare.com/privacypolicy/). The intake service does not store raw IP addresses; it uses short-lived derived values for submission rate limits. Google Analytics and Clarity do not load on the question form.

For deletion or changes to published content, contact [Leafony Shop (Japanese)](https://shop.leafony.com/pages/contact-us) with your reference number.

# Basic Kit 2: Build BLE Sensors with AVR and STM32

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/products/basic2/

Explore the leaves and accessories in Leafony Basic Kit 2, measure temperature, humidity, light and acceleration, and try AVR and STM32 BLE sensor demos.

[](https://docs.leafony.com/products/basic2/basic_kit_2_large.jpg)

## Overview

Basic Kit 2 lets you build a compact IoT sensor device that measures temperature, humidity, light and acceleration and sends the data over [Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE)](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#ble). It supports coin cell operation, and you can swap the AVR and STM32 [MCU (microcontroller)](https://docs.leafony.com/en/terms/#mcu) leaves to develop programs using the same sensors.

It includes AVR (ATmega328P) and STM32 (STM32L452REI6) MCU leaves, BLE, temperature, humidity, illuminance and acceleration sensors, and a plastic case with a magnet.

The kit ships with the AVR MCU assembled and a demo installed on each MCU. Start the [preinstalled AVR demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/basic/) without changing the stack. When you need more memory or processing capacity, you can swap in the included STM32 MCU. The [STM32 demo](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/basic2/) is an optional guide to try sensor logging and BLE communication after the swap.

  Japanese flyer. Select the image to open the full-size version in a new tab.

[View the Basic Kit 2 flyer (Japanese, A4 PDF)](https://docs.leafony.com/downloads/leafony-basic-kit-2-a4-ja.pdf)

# Cellular LPWA Cat-M1 Kit

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/products/cellular-lpwa-cat-m1/

Explore environmental sensing and cellular communication with the Cellular LPWA Cat-M1 Kit. Check its leaves, accessories, development preparation and documentation.

## Overview

This development kit combines temperature, humidity, pressure and 3-axis acceleration measurements with Cat-M1 cellular communication over mobile operators' LTE networks. It uses the AI05 environmental sensor leaf, the AP03B STM32 microcontroller leaf to run programs, and the AC09 communication leaf with a Taiyo Yuden module.

Cellular LPWA uses cellular networks for low-power IoT devices. This kit uses AC09 with Cat-M1 support and **includes a nanoSIM-compatible 1NCE SIM**. Before communicating, check the included SIM's service status, expiration date, remaining data allowance and APN, and prepare programs to control each leaf. See the [AC09 reference](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac09/) for SIM configuration examples and service requirements to check.

AV06 supplies power and accepts the included PH-connector battery holder for two AA cells.

Start with the [Cat-M1 Kit Start Guide and video](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/cellular-lpwa-cat-m1/#start-guide-video) to check additional items, assembly order and sample settings. The [Google Sheets temperature and humidity sample](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/ac09_google_sheets/) targets this kit's AP03B + AI05 + AC09 configuration.

## Watch the assembly video

## Contents

See the [kit assembly instructions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/cellular-lpwa-cat-m1/#assemble-the-kit).

### Leaves

You can replace AI05 Env Sensors with the included AX02B to prototype connections to external sensors and other circuits.

See the [AP03B STM32 MCU reference](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/processor/ap03b/) for specifications, pin connections and design documents.

### Accessories

## Development resources

- [AI05 software](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai05/#software): AP03 examples for periodic sensor readings, motion detection interrupts, and capture and waveform display of 100 acceleration samples after a shock.
- [Save temperature and humidity to Google Sheets with AC09](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/ac09_google_sheets/): Uses AP03B to read temperature and humidity from AI05's BME280 and sends them through AC09. Select the PlatformIO environment `leafony_ap03b`.

# Can AC09 send measurements to Google Sheets over cellular communication?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/ac09-google-sheets/

Sample and settings for sending BME280 temperature and humidity to Google Sheets with the Cat-M1 Kit's AP03B + AI05 + AC09 configuration.

**A sample for sending data to Google Sheets is available.** The [AC09 temperature and humidity sample](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/ac09_google_sheets/) sends temperature and humidity measured by AI05's BME280 (I2C address `0x76`) through AC09 over HTTPS to Google Apps Script, which appends them to a sheet.

AC09 sends the measurements using cellular communication (Cat-M1), an IoT technology that runs on mobile operators' LTE networks.

It targets the Cat-M1 Kit's **AP03B + AI05 + AC09** configuration using the PlatformIO environment `leafony_ap03b`. Prepare the required hardware, including a SIM, power source, and USB interface, plus a Google account, receiver-side Apps Script, destination URL, and token settings.

The Docs guide changes `SEND_INTERVAL_MS` to `600000UL` (10 minutes) between starting new readings and transmissions. The GitHub development template uses `30000UL` (30 seconds). Actual arrival intervals depend on communication conditions.

Check assembly and settings in [kit development preparation](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/cellular-lpwa-cat-m1/), then validate each stage separately.

---

# Does cellular communication with AC09 need a SIM and a service plan?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/ac09-sim/

AC09 uses a nanoSIM. Check the 1NCE or SORACOM sample settings alongside your kit and network requirements.

Yes. For cellular communication with AC09, prepare a **compatible nanoSIM, an active service plan, and the required settings**. AC09 uses Cat-M1, an IoT communication technology that runs on mobile operators' LTE networks. Even when a product includes a SIM, check its service status and configuration.

The [Cellular LPWA Cat-M1 Kit](https://docs.leafony.com/en/products/cellular-lpwa-cat-m1/#contents) **includes a nanoSIM-compatible 1NCE SIM**. When using the kit's SIM, check its service status, expiration date, remaining data allowance and APN, along with the activation instructions in the sales information.

The [AC09-to-Google-Sheets sample](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/ac09_google_sheets/) documents SIM settings for 1NCE and SORACOM (plan-D). Match settings such as the APN to your SIM.

When choosing a SIM, check:

- Cat-M1 service requirements and coverage in your area
- SIM size, activation or service status, and contract terms
- The sample’s APN settings and your MCU/communication leaf configuration

The published sample targets the Cat-M1 Kit's **AP03B + AI05 + AC09** configuration. Check your SIM's service requirements, [Cat-M1 Kit development preparation](https://docs.leafony.com/en/getting-started/cellular-lpwa-cat-m1/), and [AC09 specifications](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac09/).

---

# What supply voltage does AC09 need for cellular communication?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/ac09-voltage/

AC09 uses a 3.3V supply. For battery operation, we recommend AV06 with an external battery such as dry cells. Learn how this differs from the Basic Kit 2 coin-cell supply.

The AC09 Cat-M1 TY leaf takes power from the **3.3V Leafony Bus pin**.

AC09 uses Cat-M1, an IoT cellular communication technology that runs on mobile operators' LTE networks.

It helps to distinguish the standalone module’s specifications from those of the assembled leaf when choosing a power supply.

| Device | Power specification |
| --- | --- |
| AC09 leaf | Supply the 3.3V Leafony Bus pin (pin 1) |
| Standalone Taiyo Yuden WSCLxADAH2Z-series module | Manufacturer-specified operating range: 2.3–4.2V |

The 2.3–4.2V range applies to the standalone module, rather than the Leafony Bus input. AC09 also includes power circuits for the RF and signal sections, plus UART level conversion.

## AV06 is recommended for battery operation

For battery-powered AC09 operation, **we recommend the [AV06 1.8V–5.5V power leaf](https://shop.leafony.com/products/av06-1-8v-5-5v) with an external battery such as dry cells.** AV06 converts a 1.8–5.5V input to 3.3V for the leaves. The 1.8–5.5V range applies to the battery connected to AV06.

**The AV01 and CR2032 coin-cell supply included in Basic Kit 2 is not suitable for cellular communication with AC09.** Producing 3.3V and supplying enough current during transmission are separate requirements. If you add AC09 to Basic Kit 2, review the power configuration too.

The [published AC09 sample](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/ac09_google_sheets/) also uses AV06. [AV06 specifications](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/power/av06/) list a maximum output current of 1A, but the current available in practice also depends on the battery and input voltage. Check the battery specifications alongside the total current required by the connected leaves. Measured AC09 peak current will be announced after verification.

## References

- [AC09 specifications and power control](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac09/)
- [AV06 specifications](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/power/av06/)
- [Taiyo Yuden: cellular LPWA Cat-M1 (Japanese)](https://www.yuden.co.jp/jp/product/solutions/lpwa/)

---

# Why can I discover a BLE beacon but not connect to it?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/ble-beacon-connection/

STM32 Simple BLE Beacon is configured for reading Advertising data without a connection. It serves a different purpose from a connected receiver sample.

**If you are running STM32 Simple BLE Beacon, operating without a connection is intentional.** Discovering a device does not necessarily mean it accepts connections.

[This sample](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/stm32_simple_ble_beacon/) uses `LE_GAP_SCANNABLE_NON_CONNECTABLE`. The receiver reads Advertising data by scanning; the published code sends the device name `Leaf_A` and the text `HELLO BEACON`.

To receive sensor values after connecting or send commands to Leafony, start with a connection-based sample such as [STM32 Web Bluetooth](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/stm32_webbluetooth_iot/).

Other beacon samples and custom programs may use different connection settings and data formats. First check the name of the program running on the device.

---

# Where can I find the BLE data format and UUIDs?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/ble-data-format/

Check the sample’s transmitter and receiver code together. 4-Sensors_BLE is an example that sends comma-separated text.

**Check the transmitter and receiver code for your sample together.** Leafony does not use one universal data format; it depends on the program you upload.

In the [AVR Web Bluetooth sample](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/avr-mcu/basic/webbluetooth_iot/), `4-Sensors_BLE.ino` sends temperature, humidity, illuminance, tilt, battery voltage, and a dice value as comma-separated text. The receiver’s `handleData()` in `leafony.js` decodes UTF-8, removes line breaks, and splits the text at commas.

- **UUIDs and notifications:** Check the service and characteristic settings in the [receiver app’s source code](https://github.com/Leafony/WebBluetooth_for_Leafony_app).
- **Fields and their order:** Compare the data-generation code in your MCU sketch with the receiver’s parser.
- **Beacons:** Some samples use Advertising data instead of GATT notifications. See [STM32 Simple BLE Beacon](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/advanced/stm32-mcu/stm32/stm32_simple_ble_beacon/).

If you add fields to the transmitted data, update the receiver’s field count, order, and units as well.

---

# Should I start with Arduino IDE or PlatformIO?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/development-tools/

Choose an environment supported by your sample. Check the MCU model and sample configuration before choosing the tool.

**Start with the environment recommended by the sample you want to run.** Leafony Docs includes Arduino IDE and PlatformIO instructions for AP01, AP02, and AP03.

| Goal | A useful starting point |
| --- | --- |
| Open an `.ino` sketch and try a small sample | Arduino IDE instructions |
| Edit in VS Code and manage configuration files with the program | PlatformIO instructions |
| Reproduce an existing project | The tools and settings specified by that project |

See [Development environment](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/) for setup and [Libraries and board definitions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/) for board settings. Add sensor and communication libraries as specified by the sample.

**AP03 and AP03B are different models.** For AP03B or another MCU, check the instructions provided for that model. Using the same tool does not guarantee that board settings and pin assignments can be reused.

---

# Can I connect an external sensor?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/external-sensors/

Use an expansion leaf or the AI05 I2C header. Check power, signal levels, pin assignments, and I2C addresses.

Yes. You can choose a connection to suit the sensor’s interface and voltage.

| Connection | Typical use |
| --- | --- |
| [AX02B 29-pin](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/extension/ax02b/) | Break out the 29 Leafony Bus signals to 2.54mm-pitch pads for wiring |
| [AX06 Grove&5V](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/extension/ax06/) | Connect I2C, UART, analog, or digital signals using Grove connectors |
| J1 on [AI05 Env Sensors](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai05/) | Connect an external 3.3V I2C sensor to GND, 3.3V, SDA, and SCL |

These four points help you choose a suitable combination:

- **Supply voltage and current:** Can your power source supply the sensor?
- **Signal levels:** Do the MCU and sensor use compatible levels? A sensor’s 5V supply requirement is separate from its signal voltage. AX02B has no voltage conversion, so add level shifting where needed.
- **Pins and I2C addresses:** Are there conflicts with other leaves? For example, the AI05 accelerometer and AX06 I/O expander both use 0x18.
- **Software:** Is there a driver or library for your MCU and development environment?

For Grove sensors, checking voltage and signals alongside the connector type helps you choose a compatible device. See [Combining leaves and choosing power](https://docs.leafony.com/en/guides/combining-leaves/) for details.

## A sequence for your first test

1. Check the sensor datasheet for its interface, supply, and signal voltage, then choose a connection from the table above. For I2C, also check the [address map](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/i2c-address-map/) for conflicts with existing leaves.
2. Disconnect all power before wiring. Start with the MCU, power source, required connection leaves, and one external sensor.
3. Run a minimal sensor-reading example compatible with your MCU and check readings through serial output or a similar display.
4. Once readings work, add other leaves and processing one at a time. If an I2C sensor stops responding after an addition, see [I2C address and connection checks](https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/i2c-address-conflict/).

---

# I2C sensor stops responding after adding a leaf

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/i2c-address-conflict/

Check for duplicate I2C addresses and pull-up requirements. Combinations such as AI05 with AX06 or AC08 with AC09 need address checks.

Check for **duplicate addresses on the same I2C bus**. Devices may work individually but become impossible to address separately when another leaf uses the same address.

| Combination | Duplicate address |
| --- | --- |
| AI05 LIS2DW12 accelerometer and AX06 I/O expander | `0x18` |
| AC08 and AC09 control I/O expanders | `0x21` |

These are 7-bit addresses. Check other combinations in the [I2C address map](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/i2c-address-map/). Whether an address can be changed depends on the component and board implementation, so check each leaf’s specifications before changing only the software address.

If addresses do not overlap, also check power, signal levels, pin conflicts, and pull-up resistors. For example, AI05 R18 and R19 are not populated; with AP03, it uses the pull-ups on AP03.

## Start from the configuration that worked

Disconnect all power before changing the stack, then work through these checks.

1. **Remove the added leaf and test with the original program.** If the original configuration also fails, the added leaf may not be the only cause. Check power, contacts, wiring, and the program.
2. **Add leaves one at a time.** When readings stop, compare the pins and I2C addresses used by that combination.
3. **If addresses overlap, first use just one of those devices.** If you need both, check whether each device and board supports an address change. Changing only the software address setting does not change the actual device address.

See [Combining leaves](https://docs.leafony.com/en/guides/combining-leaves/) for a connection checklist.

---

# “No such file or directory” error when building a sample

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/library-not-found/

Match the missing header to the library specified by the sample. Similar names can refer to different authors and implementations.

Compare **the filename in the error with the library specified by your sample**. The required library may be missing, or a different implementation may be installed.

- **Arduino IDE:** Check the name and author in Library Manager. For ZIP releases, use Sketch → Include Library → Add .ZIP Library.
- **PlatformIO:** Check `lib_deps` in the active `[env:...]` section. Settings in another environment do not apply to that build.

For example, the AI04 samples use `ST7032.h` from [tomozh’s arduino_ST7032](https://github.com/tomozh/arduino_ST7032). `LCD_ST7032` and `ST7032_asukiaaa` are different libraries. Match the source rather than relying on a similar name.

[Libraries and board definitions](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/libraries/) lists common sources and installation steps. If the build still fails after installation, start with **the first error in the log** and use these checks.

| Message or situation | What to check next |
| --- | --- |
| The same header still produces `No such file or directory` | Check that the full library is installed and match its name, author, and header filename. For manual Arduino IDE installation, follow the [official instructions](https://support.arduino.cc/hc/en-us/articles/5145457742236-Install-libraries-in-the-Arduino-IDE): place the library in the sketchbook’s `libraries` folder and restart the IDE. |
| A different header is missing | Check the sample or library README for required dependencies and install them. |
| PlatformIO is building a different environment | Match the active environment name to the `[env:...]` section containing `lib_deps`. |
| The header is found, but a Core compatibility error appears | This is a different cause from a missing header. For STM32, check [Core and RTC library compatibility](https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/stm32-rtc-core/). |

---

# Can I use Python with Leafony?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/python/

On-leaf development is intended to use C/C++ with Arduino IDE, or STM32CubeIDE for STM32 leaves. Python can receive and analyze data on a PC.

**On-leaf development is intended to use C/C++ with Arduino IDE, or STM32CubeIDE for STM32 leaves.**

For Arduino samples, see the [development environment](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/). To use STM32CubeIDE and a debugger with AP03, see [connecting a debugger](https://docs.leafony.com/en/environment/stm32/stm32_debug/). Arduino sketches and CubeIDE projects use different settings and library integration, so they may require changes when moving between environments.

**Python can run on a PC to receive Leafony data, save it, plot it, and analyze it.** Write a Python receiver that matches the data sent by the C/C++ program on Leafony.

| Connection | Python options and things to check |
| --- | --- |
| Serial communication over USB | Receive data with [pySerial](https://pyserial.readthedocs.io/en/latest/shortintro.html). Upload a program that outputs serial data, then match the port, baud rate, and data format, including line endings. The leaf needed for USB connectivity depends on the MCU. |
| BLE wireless communication | Use [Bleak](https://bleak.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/client.html) to read GATT characteristics or receive notifications. Check the PC's Bluetooth environment and the sample's connection method, UUIDs, and data format. |

For USB, the [STM32 temperature and humidity sample](https://docs.leafony.com/en/examples/beginner/stm32-mcu/basic/temp_humid_sensors/) provides an example of serial output. Its baud rate is **115200 bps**. First check that values appear in Arduino IDE's serial monitor, then close the monitor before opening the same port from Python.

For BLE, use the [data format and UUID guidance](https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/ble-data-format/) to write a receiver that matches your sample. For a non-connectable beacon, scan its advertising data instead of making a GATT connection.

**To run Python on the leaf itself, you need a separate runtime such as MicroPython.** [MicroPython for ESP32](https://docs.micropython.org/en/latest/esp32/quickref.html) is available, but a supported chip alone does not mean that every Leafony leaf or sensor will work unchanged. Check the firmware for the board, pin configuration, and sensor drivers. Leafony Docs currently does not include hardware-verified MicroPython setup instructions for AP02 or AP03.

If your goal is sensor data analysis, start with **an existing Arduino sample on Leafony and Python on the PC**. Also see [programming languages for STM32](https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/stm32-language/).

---

# Are the wireless leaves certified for use in Japan?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/radio-certification/

Learn how certified module and antenna combinations work and where to check certification markings on the module.

Yes. When a certified wireless module is used with an antenna covered by its certification, within the specified conditions, customers do not need additional Japanese radio certification for that same radio equipment.

## About the module and antenna combination

Certification covers the module and antenna combination, along with conditions such as output power and frequency.

Leafony uses STAF onboard antennas as part of combinations covered by the corresponding module certification. For example, [AC08 LTE-M Mary](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac08/) uses the certified combination of Murata Type 1SC and STAF 1019-085A. [AC07 LoRa Mary](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac07/) also documents Type ABZ with the same antenna.

[AC09 Cat-M1 TY](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac09/) uses a Taiyo Yuden module and STAF 1019-085A. Taiyo Yuden states that using an antenna covered by Japanese radio certification avoids additional certification. The module model, certification number, and corresponding antenna documentation let you check a specific configuration.

## Where is the certification marking?

Look on the **wireless module itself**, mounted on the leaf. Some modules display the Japanese certification mark and number on their metal shield or other surface. “On the chip side” refers to the wireless module body here. The location and marking method vary by product; manufacturer documentation can help you find them.

If assembly hides the marking, disconnect all power before checking it. For small text, take a photo of the module surface with a smartphone or similar camera, zoom in, and compare it with the photos and module name in the leaf’s technical documentation. Distinguish the leaf model printed on the board from the module model and certification number printed on the module.

## If you would like to change the antenna

For an external antenna or changes to the radio circuit, use the manufacturer’s certification documents to check whether the new configuration is covered. Alongside connector compatibility, the antenna model and operating conditions are the key points to check.

This explanation concerns Japan’s Radio Act. Overseas certification, cellular subscriptions, and carrier compatibility can be checked separately.

## References

- [AC08 module and antenna](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac08/)
- [AC07 module and antenna](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac07/)
- [AC09 module and antenna specifications](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/communication/ac09/)
- [Taiyo Yuden: cellular LPWA Cat-M1 and certified antennas (Japanese)](https://www.yuden.co.jp/jp/product/solutions/lpwa/)

# What sensors are available?

URL: https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/sensor-options/

Explore temperature, humidity, light, acceleration, and pressure sensing with AI01 and AI05. Distinguish discontinued AI02/AI03 leaves and optional sensors.

Choose a sensor leaf according to what you want to measure, such as temperature, humidity, light, acceleration, or pressure.

| Leaf | Standard capabilities |
| --- | --- |
| [AI01 4-Sensors](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai01/) | Temperature, humidity, light, and acceleration |
| [AI05 Env Sensors](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai05/) | Temperature, humidity, and pressure (BME280), plus acceleration (LIS2DW12) |

AI05 also has locations for optional SHT40, SGP40, and BME680 components. These are not fitted as standard, so gas or air-quality measurements need a configuration that includes the additional components.

## Discontinued leaves

**AI02 and AI03 are discontinued.** The following information is for people who already own these leaves.

| Leaf | Standard capabilities |
| --- | --- |
| [AI02 SP&PIR](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai02/) (**discontinued**) | Infrared sensing for detecting a person approaching; also includes a speaker |
| [AI03 MIC&VR&LED](https://docs.leafony.com/en/leaf/io/ai03/) (**discontinued**) | Microphone input; also includes a potentiometer and LED |

Approach detection depends on installation and detection range; sound measurements also depend on microphone sensitivity and processing. The microphone example is a starting point for exploring changes in sound. Using it as a calibrated sound-level meter requires consideration of accuracy and calibration as well.

For a new project that needs approach detection or microphone input, or for other measurements, you can also [connect an external sensor](https://docs.leafony.com/en/questions/external-sensors/). Your measurement target, range, frequency, and required accuracy will help narrow down the options.
